projects.name: Reaction-time game (Sandy's first build)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from your laptop to the Uno (5V via the Uno's USB-B port). No batteries, no wall plug.
projects.description:
**Goal:** Arduino lights an LED after a random 2-5 second pause. Player slaps the button as fast as possible after the LED comes on. Reaction time prints to the Serial Monitor in milliseconds. Aiming for sub-250 ms on a good day.

**First electronics project, age 10, no soldering needed.**

## Parts list (allocated below)

- Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone)
- Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm
- 1x red 5mm LED
- 1x 220R resistor (colour bands: red-red-brown-gold)
- 1x tactile push-button, 4-pin (3x6x3.1mm)
- 4x M-M jumper wires
- USB cable for the Uno - check the clone (USB-B "square printer", mini-USB, or USB-C; grab one in advance)

## Wiring notes

See the diagram below for the circuit. When building it on the breadboard:

- The breadboard's two long side rails are usually power and ground. Use one rail as GND.
- The short rows in the middle are joined under the plastic; same row = electrically the same.
- Plug the LED so its long leg (+) and short leg (-) end up in different rows.
- The 220Ω resistor goes between the LED's short-leg row and the GND rail.
- The push-button has 4 legs but only 2 are "the switch". If pressing doesn't register, rotate the button 90° and re-seat.
- Run one M-M jumper from the Arduino GND pin to the GND rail so the whole rail is grounded.

## Talking points while he wires it up

Drip-feed one at a time, not all at once.

- **LEDs have a long leg (+) and a short leg (-).** Backwards = no light, but no damage.
- **The resistor stops the LED getting too much current** and burning out. Garden-hose analogy: too much water blows the nozzle.
- **A breadboard's short rows are joined under the plastic.** The two long rails on the sides are usually power and ground.
- **The code's `loop()` runs forever**, top to bottom, then starts again. That's why the game keeps coming back round.
- **Average human reaction time is about 250 ms.** That's the benchmark to beat.

## Things to change once it works

Give him the goal, let him hunt for the change in the code.

- Make the random pause longer or shorter.
- Cheat-detect: if the button is pressed *before* the LED lights, print "Too early!" instead of a time.
- Best-of-five mode: track and average over 5 rounds.
- Add a second LED that turns on when he beats his previous best time.

## Prep checklist for Andy

- [ ] Install the Arduino IDE from [arduino.cc](https://arduino.cc) - free, Windows.
- [ ] Plug the Uno in once yourself first. Windows will prompt for a CH340 USB driver - let it install.
- [ ] Open the IDE: **Tools -> Port** should show a COM port. Set **Tools -> Board -> Arduino Uno**.
- [ ] Confirm the USB cable type the clone uses.
- [ ] Pre-count one 220R resistor (red-red-brown-gold) so he isn't squinting at colour bands on the first try.

## Next project once he's hooked

**Wave-controlled lamp.** Same Uno, same breadboard, swap the button for the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor. LED brightens as your hand gets closer, dims as you move it away. Two extra wires and one extra component beyond this build.

projects.name: Bedroom Temperature Dashboard
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a laptop or USB charger to the XIAO (5 V on the USB rail, regulated to 3.3 V on-board)
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x XIAO ESP32-C3
- 1x USB-C cable (data-capable, plugged into a laptop or any 5 V USB charger)
- GeeFam WiFi (2.4 GHz) within range of where the XIAO sits

That is the entire bill of materials. No breadboard, no jumpers, no sensor module - the chip measures its own internal temperature.

**Before flashing:** open the sketch and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` on the `WIFI_PASSWORD` line with the real GeeFam WiFi password. The sketch will compile either way, but it cannot join the network without the real password.

## Wiring notes

There is no wiring to do. Plug the USB-C cable into the XIAO and into a laptop or a phone charger. The 5 V on the USB rail powers the XIAO; the on-board regulator drops it to 3.3 V for the ESP32-C3.

Two practical notes:

1. Use a short, known-good data cable plugged directly into the laptop (not through a hub). The XIAO is known to brown out on thin cables when the WiFi radio first kicks in.
2. The first time you upload, you may need to hold the BOOT button (next to the USB-C connector) while plugging in, to force the bootloader. After that, normal uploads should "just work".

## Talking points

- This is the first project where the XIAO does two things at once: it joins WiFi AND it answers HTTP requests from a browser. The Arduino core handles the messy networking parts so the sketch stays short.
- **Honest framing of the "sensor":** every ESP32 has a small thermal diode used internally for thermal management, and `temperatureRead()` exposes it as a Celsius value. But the chip warms itself by running, so the reading is the *chip* temperature, not the *room* temperature - it will typically sit at 40-55 C even in a cool room. The web page says this in a yellow note so nobody is confused. Honesty about what a sensor is actually measuring is a real engineering skill.
- The web page is one self-contained HTML string built in the sketch. It uses `<meta http-equiv='refresh' content='5'>` to tell the browser to reload itself every 5 seconds. No JavaScript, no separate JSON endpoint - the simplest possible "live" web page.
- Why no breadboard / resistor / external sensor? Because the goal of this project is to *just* learn how to host a web page on a microcontroller, with nothing else in the way. The next project adds the real sensor.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a real external temperature sensor like a DHT22 or BME280 to measure the *room* instead of the chip. Now it is a useful bedroom thermometer (and the page title can honestly say "Bedroom Temperature").
- Once a real sensor is in, keep the last N readings in memory and draw a small graph in the browser. (That is the natural next step up in difficulty - it adds a ring buffer, JSON, and HTML canvas drawing.)
- Have the XIAO publish each reading over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once the Pi is booted). That is the bridge from "one device with a webpage" to "a real home-automation network".

## Why this is interesting

This is the smallest possible "real" IoT project: a device on the network that you open in a browser like any other website. Once Andy sees a temperature reading updating in Chrome that is being served by a thumbnail-sized chip on his desk, the rest of the kit makes sense - the ESP32s are tiny web servers / data sources, and the Orange Pi will eventually be the always-on hub that collects from all of them. It also reuses the already-working WiFi connect logic from `XIAO_ESP32C3/Wifi/connect-wifi.ino`, so the only new idea is "host a page".

projects.name: Mood Meter (touch the dot, change your face)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop to the XIAO ESP32-C3 (5V in, regulated to 3.3V on-board; 3.3V powers the OLED and the TTP223B via the breadboard rails)
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - runs the sketch, drives the screen)
- 1x 0.96" SSD1306 OLED, I2C version (4 pins: VCC, GND, SCL, SDA)
- 1x TTP223B capacitive touch module (3 pins: VCC, GND, I/O)
- 1x breadboard (shared 3.3V and GND rails)
- 8x F-M jumper wires (XIAO header to breadboard rails and modules)

## Wiring notes

Everything in this project runs on 3.3V. The XIAO ESP32-C3 is a 3.3V board, the SSD1306 OLED works happily on 3.3V (it actually prefers it), and the TTP223B is rated for 2-5.5V. Do NOT use the 5V pin on the XIAO for any of this.

Power rails on the breadboard:
- Red rail: XIAO 3V3 pin -> red (+) rail
- Black rail: XIAO GND pin -> blue (-) rail

OLED (I2C):
- VCC -> red rail (3.3V)
- GND -> blue rail
- SDA -> XIAO D4 (GPIO 6)
- SCL -> XIAO D5 (GPIO 7)

TTP223B touch module:
- VCC -> red rail (3.3V)
- GND -> blue rail
- I/O (sometimes labeled SIG or OUT) -> XIAO D0 (GPIO 2)

The TTP223B's I/O pin sits LOW when nothing is touching the pad and goes HIGH when a finger lands on the metal area on top of the module. No pull-up or pull-down resistor needed - the chip handles that internally.

Two tiny gotchas worth knowing:
1. The OLED address is usually 0x3C but a few clones are 0x3D - if the screen stays blank, that's the first thing to swap in the code.
2. The first time the TTP223B powers on it spends ~0.5s calibrating "what counts as not-touched". Don't keep your finger on the pad while you press reset.

## Talking points

- I2C uses just two wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and can talk to up to ~120 devices in theory. The OLED listens on address 0x3C; if we added a second I2C gadget (temperature sensor, real-time clock, another screen) it would share the same two wires with a different address.
- "Capacitive touch" means the chip is measuring how much electrical charge the pad can hold. A finger nearby adds a tiny bit of capacitance, the chip notices the change, and flips the output pin. No moving parts, no wear.
- The face is drawn from primitives: `drawCircle`, `drawLine`, `fillCircle`, plus a couple of stray pixels for the smile curl. It's the same toolbox an old 8-bit game would have used.

## Things to change once it works

- Add more moods. Adding a fifth case is one enum entry, one name string, one extra `case` in `drawFace`, and bumping the modulo from 4 to 5.
- Make the eyes blink every few seconds when idle (timer + extra draw call).
- Connect to WiFi (SSID `GeeFam`, password `PASSWORD_HERE`) and pull the real time from an NTP server so the log timestamp is a clock time instead of seconds-since-boot.
- Hold-to-confirm: instead of cycling on every tap, require a 300ms hold so accidental brushes don't change the face.
- Once the Orange Pi is running Mosquitto, publish each mood change as an MQTT message - first cross-device milestone for the kit.

## Why this is interesting

Two of the most useful "building block" skills for everything else in the kit live in this project: talking to an I2C peripheral, and reacting to a non-button input. Once OLED graphics feel familiar, every future sensor reading (temperature, distance, humidity) has somewhere nice to show up. And capacitive touch is the gateway to projects that don't look like electronics at all - hidden touch points behind wood, glass, or a 3D-printed shell.

<![CDATA[// Mood Meter - touch the dot, change your face
// Hardware: XIAO ESP32-C3 + SSD1306 0.96" I2C OLED + TTP223B touch module
//
// Libraries to install via Arduino IDE Library Manager:
//   - Adafruit GFX Library
//   - Adafruit SSD1306
//
// Board: "XIAO_ESP32C3" (under ESP32 Arduino)
// Serial baud: 115200

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>

// ---- Pin assignments (match the wiring diagram) ----
// XIAO ESP32-C3 default I2C pins:
//   SDA = GPIO 6  (silkscreen "D4")
//   SCL = GPIO 7  (silkscreen "D5")
// TTP223B signal:
//   TOUCH = GPIO 2 (silkscreen "D0")
const int PIN_TOUCH = 2;

// ---- Display setup ----
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET   -1     // share the XIAO reset
#define OLED_ADDR    0x3C   // most cheap 0.96" SSD1306 boards
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// ---- Mood state ----
enum Mood { HAPPY = 0, SLEEPY = 1, GRUMPY = 2, SURPRISED = 3 };
const char* MOOD_NAMES[4] = { "happy", "sleepy", "grumpy", "surprised" };
Mood currentMood = HAPPY;

// ---- Touch debounce ----
int lastTouchState = LOW;
unsigned long lastTouchChangeMs = 0;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 50;

// ---- Timestamp (seconds since boot - good enough without WiFi) ----
unsigned long lastChangeSec = 0;

// ---------- Drawing helpers ----------

// Draw the face inside a circle in the upper portion of the screen.
// Center at (64, 24), radius 20. That leaves the bottom for the log line.
void drawFace(Mood m) {
  const int cx = 64;
  const int cy = 24;
  const int r  = 20;

  // outline of the face
  display.drawCircle(cx, cy, r, SSD1306_WHITE);

  // eyes - default position
  int eyeLx = cx - 7;
  int eyeRx = cx + 7;
  int eyeY  = cy - 5;

  switch (m) {
    case HAPPY:
      // round eyes
      display.fillCircle(eyeLx, eyeY, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeRx, eyeY, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // smile - arc-ish: a short horizontal line with curled ends
      display.drawLine(cx - 6, cy + 4, cx + 6, cy + 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx - 7, cy + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx + 7, cy + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;

    case SLEEPY:
      // closed eyes - horizontal lines
      display.drawLine(eyeLx - 3, eyeY, eyeLx + 3, eyeY, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawLine(eyeRx - 3, eyeY, eyeRx + 3, eyeY, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // tiny "o" mouth
      display.drawCircle(cx, cy + 5, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // a little "Z" floating up-right
      display.setTextSize(1);
      display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.setCursor(cx + r - 4, cy - r);
      display.print("z");
      break;

    case GRUMPY:
      // angled eyebrows over round eyes
      display.drawLine(eyeLx - 4, eyeY - 4, eyeLx + 3, eyeY - 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawLine(eyeRx + 4, eyeY - 4, eyeRx - 3, eyeY - 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeLx, eyeY + 1, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeRx, eyeY + 1, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // frown - line that curves the other way
      display.drawLine(cx - 6, cy + 7, cx + 6, cy + 7, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx - 7, cy + 8, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx + 7, cy + 8, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;

    case SURPRISED:
      // wide round eyes
      display.drawCircle(eyeLx, eyeY, 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawCircle(eyeRx, eyeY, 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // open "O" mouth
      display.drawCircle(cx, cy + 7, 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;
  }
}

// Format seconds-since-boot as M:SS so the log line looks like a timestamp.
void formatTimestamp(unsigned long totalSec, char* out, size_t outLen) {
  unsigned long minutes = totalSec / 60;
  unsigned long seconds = totalSec % 60;
  snprintf(out, outLen, "%lu:%02lu", minutes, seconds);
}

void drawLogLine() {
  char ts[16];
  formatTimestamp(lastChangeSec, ts, sizeof(ts));

  display.setTextSize(1);
  display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);

  // bottom log area: line + text
  display.drawLine(0, 50, SCREEN_WIDTH - 1, 50, SSD1306_WHITE);
  display.setCursor(2, 54);
  display.print("[");
  display.print(ts);
  display.print("] ");
  display.print(MOOD_NAMES[currentMood]);
}

void redraw() {
  display.clearDisplay();
  drawFace(currentMood);
  drawLogLine();
  display.display();
}

// ---------- Arduino entry points ----------

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(300);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Mood Meter starting...");

  pinMode(PIN_TOUCH, INPUT);

  // Start I2C on the XIAO's default SDA=6, SCL=7
  Wire.begin();

  if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDR)) {
    Serial.println("SSD1306 not found at 0x3C - check wiring");
    while (true) {
      delay(1000);
    }
  }

  display.clearDisplay();
  display.setTextSize(1);
  display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
  display.setCursor(0, 0);
  display.println("Mood Meter ready.");
  display.println("Touch to cycle...");
  display.display();
  delay(800);

  redraw();
}

void loop() {
  int reading = digitalRead(PIN_TOUCH);

  // Debounced edge detection - act on LOW -> HIGH transition (touch start)
  if (reading != lastTouchState) {
    if (millis() - lastTouchChangeMs >= DEBOUNCE_MS) {
      lastTouchChangeMs = millis();

      if (reading == HIGH) {
        // Cycle to next mood
        currentMood = static_cast<Mood>((static_cast<int>(currentMood) + 1) % 4);
        lastChangeSec = millis() / 1000UL;

        Serial.print("Mood -> ");
        Serial.print(MOOD_NAMES[currentMood]);
        Serial.print(" at ");
        Serial.print(lastChangeSec);
        Serial.println("s");

        redraw();
      }
      lastTouchState = reading;
    }
  }

  delay(5);
}

projects.description:
## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the sensor, blinks the LED)
- HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (the "eye" that bounces sound off your hand)
- 5mm red LED (the visible heartbeat)
- 220R resistor (current limiter for the LED - keeps it from burning out)
- 1K resistor + 2.2K resistor (voltage divider on the Echo line - see Wiring notes)
- Breadboard, 400 tie-points
- A handful of male-male jumper wires
- A USB cable from your laptop to the ESP32 (power and code-upload in one)

## Wiring notes

**The HC-SR04 runs on 5V, but the ESP32 is a 3.3V chip.** Powering the sensor from the ESP32's VIN pin (which mirrors the USB 5V rail on most NodeMCU-32S boards - some silkscreens label this pin `5V` or `VBUS` instead of `VIN`, and on a few revisions VIN sits behind a Schottky diode so it reads ~4.7V; any of those is fine for the HC-SR04) is the easy option. But the sensor's Echo pin will swing up to 5V, and that's too much for the ESP32 GPIO. The fix is a tiny voltage divider made of two resistors:

- Sensor Echo -> 1K resistor -> ESP32 GPIO 18 (this junction is what the ESP32 reads)
- From that same junction -> 2.2K resistor -> GND

That divider pulls the 5V Echo signal down to roughly 3.4V at the ESP32 pin. Trig is an output FROM the ESP32 to the sensor, so 3.3V is usually enough to drive it - no divider needed there. **Caveat:** a small minority of HC-SR04 clones (especially newer ones with stricter input thresholds) won't trigger reliably from a 3.3V Trig signal. The symptom is that distance reads -1 ("no echo") even when an object is clearly in front of the sensor. The fix is to drive Trig through a level shifter, or use a 5V-tolerant logic source - but try the simple wiring first.

**LED side:** the long leg of the LED (anode, +) goes through the 220R resistor to GPIO 19. The short leg (cathode, -) goes to a GND rail. The resistor can be on either side of the LED - it's there to limit the current, the LED doesn't care which side.

**Pins used:**

- GPIO 5  -> HC-SR04 Trig
- GPIO 18 -> HC-SR04 Echo (through the voltage divider)
- GPIO 19 -> LED anode (through the 220R resistor)
- 5V (VIN) -> HC-SR04 VCC
- GND -> HC-SR04 GND, LED cathode, and the bottom of the voltage divider

## Talking points

- **How ultrasonic distance works:** the sensor chirps a 40kHz "click" your ears can't hear, then listens for the echo. The ESP32 times how long the click takes to come back. Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air, so distance in cm = duration in microseconds * 0.0343 / 2 (the "divide by 2" is because the sound made a round trip).
- **Why the LED gets faster when your hand gets closer:** the code maps distance to a blink delay. Far away -> long delay -> slow blink. Close -> short delay -> rapid pulse. That mapping is a simple linear interpolation (lerp).
- **Why three resistors for one LED:** one limits LED current (220R), the other two protect the ESP32 from 5V on its Echo input. Two different jobs.
- **Why GPIO 5/18/19:** these are "safe" output pins on the ESP32. Some pins (like 0, 2, 12, 15) are tied to boot behaviour and pulling them HIGH or LOW at startup can prevent the board from booting. Sticking to 5, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23 avoids that whole class of headache.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap the LED for the onboard blue LED on GPIO 2 (one less wire on the breadboard).
- Print distance to the Serial Monitor (115200 baud) so you can see numbers next to the blinking.
- Add a buzzer in parallel with the LED for an actual Geiger-counter sound effect.
- Use `ledcWrite` (PWM) instead of digital ON/OFF to make the LED smoothly fade brighter as your hand approaches, instead of blinking.
- Hook three LEDs (green / yellow / red) and light them like a traffic light based on distance bands.

## Why this is interesting

This is the smallest possible bridge between the physical world and code. There are no buttons, no switches - you wave your hand in mid-air, sound waves bounce, and a light reacts. That's the same loop every smart device on Earth runs: sense, decide, act. Once this works, every other sensor in the kit (PIR motion, photoresistor, tilt switch, IR obstacle) becomes "the same project with a different sensor block at the top."

projects.description:
## Parts list

- **ESP32 NodeMCU-32S** - the brain. Watches the wand and updates the score.
- **4-digit 7-segment Display Module (TM1637, 4-pin: VCC/GND/CLK/DIO)** - shows the strike count. Powered from 5V (see wiring notes).
- **LED 5mm Red + 220R resistor** - lights while the wand is touching the wire.
- **LED 5mm Green + 220R resistor** - lights while the wand is in the clear.
- **Tactile Push-button Switch (3x6x4.3mm, white pin)** - reset-to-zero button.
- **Stiff bare wire (~30 cm)** bent into a wavy track. **Wand loop (~3 cm)** of the same wire on a short insulated handle. (Both physical-craft parts, not on the board.)
- **Heat-shrink tubing / electrical tape / pen barrel** - the insulated handle for the wand so the player's hand doesn't complete the circuit.
- **Breadboard + jumper wires** to hold everything together.

## Wiring notes

The whole game is one big switch: the bent maze wire goes to GPIO 23 with the ESP32's internal **pull-up** enabled, so the pin idles HIGH (3.3 V). The wand loop goes straight to **GND**. The instant the loop touches the maze wire, GPIO 23 is dragged to LOW - that's our "you touched it!" signal.

- Maze wire -> long jumper to GPIO 23 (INPUT_PULLUP).
- Wand loop -> long jumper to a GND rail on the breadboard.
- Red LED: GPIO 18 -> 220R -> LED anode -> LED cathode -> GND.
- Green LED: GPIO 19 -> 220R -> LED anode -> LED cathode -> GND.
- Reset button: one leg to GPIO 5 (INPUT_PULLUP), the leg diagonally opposite to GND. The other two pins are the internal short; ignore them.
- 7-segment module (TM1637): **VCC -> VIN (5 V from the USB rail)**, GND -> GND, CLK -> GPIO 22, DIO -> GPIO 21.

**Why VIN, not 3V3, for the TM1637:** these modules are spec'd for 5 V. At 3.3 V many clones run dim or flicker. The NodeMCU-32S exposes the USB 5 V rail on its VIN pin, which is the right home for the display. The CLK/DIO lines on the module idle at 5 V through pull-ups - the ESP32 is rated as 5 V-tolerant on these GPIOs in practice, and using a TM1637 this way is the standard beginner wiring.

**Heads-up on GPIO 5:** it's an ESP32 "strapping pin" - the chip looks at it during boot. With INPUT_PULLUP and the button wired to GND, it idles HIGH (released), which matches what the chip wants at boot. Safe. Just don't later wire something to GPIO 5 that holds it LOW at power-on, or the board will refuse to start and you'll wonder why.

The ESP32 itself is powered by the USB cable from the laptop; the display takes 5 V from VIN, and the LEDs / button take their references from GND.

## Talking points

- **Pull-ups in one sentence:** "The pin is held HIGH by a tiny resistor inside the chip until something outside drags it LOW. We use the wand-to-maze contact as the thing that drags it LOW." If you skip the pull-up, the pin is *floating* - touching nothing, but picking up stray noise from the air - and you'll see random ghost strikes with the wand sitting still. The pull-up is what makes "not touching" a definite, repeatable state.
- **Why a resistor on every LED:** an LED is basically a short-circuit with a glow, so the resistor sets the current. A red LED drops about 2.0 V, so across a 220R resistor on a 3.3 V GPIO the current is (3.3 - 2.0) / 220 = about **6 mA**. That's gentle - plenty visible as an indicator, well under the ESP32's ~20 mA-per-pin comfort limit. If you ever want it brighter, drop to 150R for about 8.7 mA, or move the LED to the 5 V VIN rail (still through the resistor) for around 13 mA.
- **Edge detection:** we only count a strike on the *moment* of contact - the HIGH-to-LOW transition - not every single loop where the pin happens to be LOW. That way, holding the wand against the wire doesn't rack up hundreds of strikes; one touch = one strike, no matter how long you linger.
- **Debouncing (the lighter version):** real metal contacts are jittery and can register as a few touches in 1 ms. After the edge fires we wait 20 ms and re-check; if the pin is still LOW it was a real touch, not noise. For the reset button it's even simpler: a 50 ms `delay()` before a second read. We can get away with that because nothing time-critical is happening during a reset press.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer (when one shows up in inventory) on GPIO 4 for the actual "bzzzt" sound.
- Use the reset button held for 2 seconds as "hard reset to zero" and a short tap as "new round."
- Add a timer: count seconds until the player either finishes (touches a designated "end pad" wire) or hits the max strikes. Display the time on the 7-segment between rounds.
- Wire two maze wires in parallel and use both ends as "start pad" and "end pad" so the game knows when the run is complete.
- Upgrade to a millis()-based non-blocking loop once the game logic is comfortable - that's a natural next step into intermediate territory.

## Why this is interesting

It's the smallest possible useful circuit - "two pieces of metal that complete a circuit when they touch" - dressed up as a game. The maze itself is the sensor. There's no module hiding the physics; the kid can see exactly *why* the score ticks, because they watched you bend the wire that does it. It also turns two software concepts (pull-ups and edge detection) into something tangible: without the pull-up the score creeps up on its own, and without edge detection holding the wand still while touching racks up dozens of strikes. Add them both and the game suddenly feels fair. Great moment.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the servo).
- 1x DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor module (3-pin breakout: VCC / DATA / GND).
- 1x SG90 Servo (the moving needle).
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (gives the XIAO and DHT11 a home and shared power rails).
- 1x 470uF electrolytic capacitor (sits across 5V and GND near the servo to absorb its current spikes).
- 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc pack (servo lead and DHT11 module both need female-ended jumpers to reach the breadboard).
- 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc pack (a few short wires for the 5V, 3V3 and GND rails on the breadboard).
- Craft supplies (not in inventory, grab from a drawer): a square of cardboard, a marker, a thin cardboard strip for the needle, sticky tape.

## Wiring notes

The XIAO has two power-out pins: `5V` (passthrough from the USB-C jack) and `3V3` (the on-board regulator). It matters which one we use for each part:

- The SG90 servo really wants 5V. Its motor and coil are spec'd for 4.8-6V; on 3.3V it would be weak and twitchy.
- The DHT11 module is happy anywhere from 3.0V to 5.5V, so we run it from `3V3`. That keeps its DATA line at 3.3V, which matches the XIAO's GPIO. If we powered the DHT11 from 5V, its DATA pin would idle at 5V too and we'd be pushing 5V into a 3.3V-only GPIO - that's the level-shifting problem the talking points mention. Running the sensor at 3V3 sidesteps it entirely with zero extra parts.

1. Plug the XIAO into the breadboard so each row of pins lands on its own column.
2. Run M-M jumpers to build three rails:
   - XIAO `5V` -> red (+) rail (for the servo only).
   - XIAO `3V3` -> orange tie-strip a few rows over (for the DHT11 only). Most breadboards only have two power rails, so just pick an unused row and call it the 3V3 rail - the DHT11 is the only thing that touches it.
   - XIAO `GND` -> blue (-) rail (shared by everything).
3. DHT11 module pins:
   - `VCC` (or `+`) -> the **3V3** rail (NOT the red 5V rail).
   - `GND` (or `-`) -> blue rail (GND).
   - `DATA` (or `OUT`) -> XIAO `D2` (GPIO 4).
4. SG90 servo wires:
   - Red -> red rail (5V).
   - Brown (or black) -> blue rail (GND).
   - Orange (or yellow) -> XIAO `D3` (GPIO 5).
5. The 470uF capacitor. Look for the stripe with a "-" on the side - that's the negative leg. Plug the negative leg into the blue (GND) rail and the other leg into the red (5V) rail, as close to where the servo's red and brown wires plug in as possible. This little reservoir tops up the rail during the brief instant the servo motor jerks and would otherwise sag the 5V supply.
6. Tape a thin cardboard arrow onto the servo horn. Draw a half-circle gauge on a bigger piece of cardboard and label five equal-width zones across the sweep: BRRR / CHILLY / NICE / TOASTY / LAVA. Tape the servo behind the gauge so the arrow points through a slot.

If the servo still twitches at startup and the XIAO browns out (the on-board LED blinks oddly or the serial monitor restarts), check that the capacitor's negative leg really is on GND, then try a known-good USB cable plugged directly into the computer rather than a hub. The cap handles the spike; the cable handles the steady draw.

## Talking points

- The DHT11 is "one-wire-ish": you ask, and one wiggling pin gives back both temperature and humidity. The Adafruit DHT library does all the timing for us.
- A servo isn't told a speed - it's told an angle. We `map()` Celsius into degrees so 15 C -> 0 deg, 30 C -> 180 deg.
- The DHT11 is slow. It only updates about once a second and only in whole degrees (no half-steps), so we read it once every two seconds and slowly nudge the servo toward the new angle. That avoids the dial jittering on tiny readings.
- Why a capacitor near the servo? When the servo motor starts moving, it grabs a big gulp of current for a split second. A thin USB cable can't deliver that fast enough, so the 5V rail dips, the XIAO sees a brown-out, and the whole board can reset. The cap is a tiny bucket of charge sitting right next to the servo - the servo drinks from the bucket, then the USB cable refills the bucket more slowly. Same idea as a header tank in a plumbing system.
- 3.3V vs 5V picking sides: running the DHT11 at 3V3 means its DATA line idles at 3.3V (safe for the XIAO). Running the SG90 at 5V keeps the motor strong. Each part gets the voltage it likes, and the XIAO's 3.3V signal is enough to tell the servo where to go.

## Things to change once it works

- Change the temperature range in `MIN_TEMP_C` / `MAX_TEMP_C` to match the room - if it never gets to 30 C indoors, narrow the range so the needle uses the whole gauge. Re-space the mood thresholds in `moodFor()` to match, keeping them equal-width.
- Add humidity to the dial too - print it to serial first, then maybe a second servo for "DRY / OK / SWAMP".
- Smooth the reading by averaging the last few values before mapping to an angle.
- Swap the DHT11 for a DHT22 or BMP280 later for finer-grained readings (the DHT11 only reports whole degrees, which is why the serial line shows no decimal).

## Why this is interesting

It turns an invisible thing (room temperature) into a physical, kid-friendly object that moves. The cardboard gauge is the canvas - Andy and his son can re-draw it as a volcano, a dragon's mouth, a thermometer in a desert, anything. The electronics underneath stay the same; the storytelling on top is theirs.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the shake sensor and drives the display)
- SW-420 vibration switch module (digital "did something shake?" sensor)
- 4-digit 7-segment display module (TM1637 driver - only needs two data pins)
- 1x 5mm green LED + 1x 220 ohm resistor (lights up while the dice is "rolling")
- Breadboard + DuPont jumper wires
- Micro-USB cable from your laptop to power the ESP32

## Wiring notes

The ESP32 sits across the breadboard's centre gutter. Both side rails get jumpered to the ESP32: one rail is 3.3V, the other is GND.

**Power rails**
- ESP32 `3V3` pin -> red rail on the breadboard
- ESP32 `GND` pin -> blue (ground) rail on the breadboard

**SW-420 vibration module** (3 pins: VCC, GND, DO)
- VCC -> 3.3V red rail
- GND -> blue ground rail
- DO  -> ESP32 GPIO27

GPIO27 is a regular general-purpose pin on the ESP32. We deliberately avoided GPIO12, GPIO14 and a couple of others called "strapping pins" - those control how the chip boots, and a sensor pulling them around at power-on can confuse the boot process.

The SW-420 is essentially a digital switch. It sits HIGH normally and flickers LOW when the little spring inside gets jostled. The board has a sensitivity trimpot you can twist with a small screwdriver if it's too touchy or not touchy enough.

**TM1637 4-digit display** (4 pins: CLK, DIO, VCC, GND)
- VCC -> 3.3V red rail
- GND -> blue ground rail
- CLK -> ESP32 GPIO18
- DIO -> ESP32 GPIO19

These modules are happy on 3.3V even though most listings say 5V. Two data pins is all it takes - the TM1637 chip on the back of the module handles the actual segment timing.

**Green LED** (the "rolling" indicator)
- Long leg (anode) -> 220 ohm resistor -> ESP32 GPIO26
- Short leg (cathode) -> blue ground rail

The resistor goes BEFORE the LED, on the GPIO side. The order doesn't matter electrically, but it's a good habit.

## Talking points

- **Why the SW-420 is "noisy":** one shake makes the spring inside rattle on and off many times. The code handles this with a classic two-step debounce: read once, wait 50 ms for the bouncing to settle, read again. If both reads agree, it was a real shake. The exact same trick works for noisy push buttons.
- **Why the dice slows down:** the animation array `delays[]` has shorter delays at the start and longer ones at the end. That alone makes it feel like a real tumbling die. No physics needed.
- **Where the randomness comes from:** `esp_random()` uses the ESP32's hardware random number generator. On an Arduino Uno you'd have to "seed" the random function with noise from a floating pin - on the ESP32 you get true hardware randomness for free.
- **Why 3.3V is fine for all of this:** the TM1637 chip is happy from 3.3V to 5.5V, the SW-420 just needs enough voltage to drive a logic-level signal, and the LED is comfortable too. Worth knowing: at 3.3V drive with a 220 ohm resistor and a typical green LED (forward voltage ~2V), the LED current is about (3.3 - 2) / 220 = 6 mA, which is visible but not super bright. If you want the announce-blink to really pop, swap to a 150 ohm resistor - that pushes the current up to ~9 mA, still well under the LED's limit.

## Things to change once it works

- Twist the sensitivity trimpot on the SW-420 so it triggers from a firm shake but ignores you bumping the table.
- Show the previous roll in the leftmost digits and the new roll on the right - the display has 4 digits, you're only using 1.
- Add a second LED that lights up only when you roll a 6 (a "critical hit" indicator).
- Replace the dice with a 2d6 simulator (two dice at once, one per pair of digits) for board games.
- Add a piezo buzzer that beeps faster and faster as the roll slows down.

## Why this is interesting

You're replacing a physical object (a die) with code, but the *feel* of using it is what makes it work - the spin-down animation tricks your brain into accepting it as a real roll. That's the core lesson of human-computer interaction in one tiny project: the math is trivial (`random() % 6 + 1`), but the perceived experience is everything.

It also introduces a sensor that isn't a button or a knob. Once you've used the SW-420, you understand the general pattern for "event-driven" sensors: read, debounce, then act.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - the brain. Reads the PIR, blinks the LED, twitches the servo.
- 1x HC-SR501 PIR Motion Sensor - the "eye". Detects warm bodies moving past.
- 1x SG90 Servo (9g micro) - the muscle. Tape it under the lid; horn flips the lid open.
- 1x 5mm Red LED - "armed" indicator so you know the trap is live.
- 1x 220R resistor - current-limiter for the LED so it does not burn out.
- 1x 470 uF electrolytic capacitor - soaks up the servo's start-up current spike so the ESP32 does not brown out and reset when the lid snaps. Long leg (+) to the 5V rail, short leg (-) to GND. Polarity matters - backwards can pop the cap.
- 1x Breadboard - holds the LED, resistor, capacitor, and power rails.
- Jumper wires (F-M for the PIR/servo headers, M-M for breadboard hops).
- USB cable from laptop to power the ESP32.
- (Not in the inventory) a small cardboard box and a paper spider on a spring or rubber band.

## One-time software setup

Before this sketch will compile, install the **ESP32Servo** library:

1. Arduino IDE -> Tools -> Manage Libraries...
2. Search for `ESP32Servo` (by Kevin Harrington / John K. Bennett).
3. Click Install. Done - this is a one-time step.

If you skip this you will get `ESP32Servo.h: No such file or directory` when you try to upload.

## Wiring notes

- The HC-SR501 is a 5V module. Wire its VCC to the ESP32 `VIN` pin (the raw rail coming back out of the USB port), and GND to any ESP32 GND. Its OUT pin only swings up to ~3.3V, so it is safe to feed straight into ESP32 GPIO 13 - no level shifter, no resistor divider.
- The SG90 also runs from 5V. Red wire to `VIN`, brown wire to GND, orange (signal) to **GPIO 25**. The ESP32 GPIO is 3.3V, but the SG90 signal pin reads a 3.3V pulse just fine.
- Place the 470 uF capacitor on the breadboard right next to where the servo's red and brown wires plug in. Long leg goes into the 5V rail row, short leg goes into the GND rail row. This is the single most important non-obvious part of the build - skipping it is what makes "lid snaps, ESP32 reboots, sketch starts over" happen.
- The LED has a long leg (anode, +) and a short leg (cathode, -). Long leg goes through the 220R resistor to GPIO 27. Short leg goes to a GND rail.
- The PIR has two orange potentiometers on the back. Start with **sensitivity** turned roughly to the middle and **time delay** turned all the way counter-clockwise (shortest hold, ~3 seconds). There is also a jumper on the side with positions **H** and **L**:
  - **L** (single trigger / non-retriggerable) - the PIR fires once per motion event, then forces a quiet period. This is what we want so the box does not keep firing while you walk past.
  - **H** (repeatable / retriggerable) - the PIR keeps re-asserting HIGH as long as it sees movement, restarting its hold timer each time. Useful for "porch light stays on while someone is there" but wrong for a one-shot scare. Set the jumper to **L**.
- The PIR needs ~30-60 seconds to "warm up" after power-on. During warm-up it can output false HIGHs - the sketch deliberately ignores motion for the first 60 seconds and the LED blinks fast to tell you it is warming up.

## A note on USB power

The ESP32's `VIN` pin is *not* a clean 5V. After the USB connector and the board's protection diode, you typically see 4.5-4.7 V under load. That is fine for an LED and a PIR, and the SG90 will move on it, but the servo will be a little weaker than its datasheet rating and the PIR can occasionally false-trigger on the supply dip. If the lid feels gutless or the box keeps firing on its own, the upgrade is a separate 5V phone-charger-style supply feeding the servo (with its GND tied to the ESP32's GND). For learning on the desk, USB-from-laptop plus the 470 uF cap is fine.

## Talking points

- A PIR (Passive InfraRed) sensor does not emit anything. It just watches for *changes* in infrared (heat) hitting its dome. If a warm body crosses one zone but not the next, the chip flags motion.
- A hobby servo does not turn freely - it goes to a specific *angle* between 0 and 180 degrees and holds it. So "open the lid" is "go to 120 degrees" and "reset" is "go back to 0 degrees".
- Servos draw a big current spike when they first start moving (the SG90 can briefly pull 600-700 mA, several times its idle draw). Without help, that spike pulls the 5V rail down, the ESP32 sees a brown-out, and resets. The 470 uF capacitor is a tiny local "battery" right next to the servo: it dumps stored charge to cover the spike, then refills from USB.
- The ESP32 has lots of GPIOs but they are not all equivalent. Some are **strapping pins** (0, 2, 4, 5, 12, 15) that the chip reads at boot to decide how to start - and a few of them also pulse PWM-like signals during boot. **GPIO 14** is one of those boot-noisy pins, which is why we put the servo on **GPIO 25** instead. GPIO 25, 26, 32 and 33 are quiet at boot and a good default choice for actuators. GPIO 13 (PIR input) and GPIO 27 (LED) are also safely behaved.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a small piezo buzzer on another GPIO and play a scream when the lid pops.
- Build a paper spider on a thin spring so the lid-flip also launches it upward instead of just opening the lid.
- Lengthen the cool-down in code so the box only fires once every 30 seconds (no double-spooking).
- Move from USB-from-laptop power to a proper 5V supply (phone charger + USB cable, or a barrel-jack 5V brick into VIN) so the servo gets its full punch.
- Once the Orange Pi is up, send an MQTT message every time the box fires so you get a phone notification "the trap got someone".

## Why this is interesting

This is the simplest possible "sensor sees something -> something physical happens" loop, which is the core idea of every home-automation project. There is no WiFi yet, no app, no cloud. Just: read a digital pin, decide, move a motor. Once this works, every future project is a variation: swap the PIR for a door sensor, swap the servo for a relay, swap the spider for a light switch.

projects.description:
## Parts list

From the kit:

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the Hall sensor, blinks the LED, drives the display)
- 1x KY-024 Linear Magnetic Hall Sensor (4-pin: A0 analog out, D0 digital out, +, -). This is the *linear* Hall sensor - its analog output voltage swings up or down depending on the magnet's pole and how close it is. We only use the A0 (analog) pin.
- 1x 4-digit 7-segment Display Module (TM1637-based, 4 pins: VCC, GND, DIO, CLK)
- 1x LED 5mm Red (any colour works, red is most visible against couch cushions)
- 1x Resistor 220R 1/8W 1% (the LED's bodyguard - keeps it from burning out)
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points)
- 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc bundle (for breadboard-to-breadboard hops)
- 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc bundle (for ESP32 header pin to breadboard, and to the KY-024 / TM1637 modules)

You supply:

- 1x small neodymium magnet - the "treasure". A fridge magnet works in a pinch; a small neodymium is much more dramatic.
- 1x USB cable (laptop to ESP32 NodeMCU-32S, micro-USB).

## Libraries to install

Open Arduino IDE > Tools > Manage Libraries... and install:

- **TM1637Display** by Avishay Orpaz - drives the 4-digit display.

## Wiring notes

The ESP32 NodeMCU-32S has plenty of pins. We're using:

- GPIO 34 -> KY-024 A0 (analog signal). GPIO 34 is an input-only ADC pin, perfect for reading an analog voltage. We ignore the D0 (digital) pin entirely.
- 3.3V -> KY-024 + (the KY-024 is happy on 3.3V)
- GND -> KY-024 -
- GPIO 2 -> 220 ohm resistor -> LED anode (long leg), then LED cathode to GND.
- GPIO 22 -> TM1637 CLK
- GPIO 21 -> TM1637 DIO
- 3.3V -> TM1637 VCC (these modules run fine on 3.3V)
- GND -> TM1637 GND

**About GPIO 2:** GPIO 2 is also the onboard blue LED, so you'll see the onboard one mirror the external red one - free bonus. GPIO 2 is also a "strapping pin" the ESP32 reads at power-on to decide its boot mode. The pin must be LOW (or floating) at boot for normal program execution. The sketch deliberately calls `digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW)` *before* `pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT)` in `setup()` so that the moment the pin becomes an output it's already low, which keeps the strapping condition correct. Don't reorder those two lines.

With no magnet near the KY-024, the analog reading sits around the midpoint (~1900-2100 on a 0-4095 scale). As a magnet approaches, the value swings up OR down depending on which pole of the magnet faces the sensor's flat side. The sketch tracks the absolute distance from the resting baseline, so either pole works.

## Talking points

- Magnetic fields are invisible but the LED makes them visible - that's the whole magic moment.
- The sensor uses the "Hall effect": moving electrons in the sensor get pushed sideways by a magnetic field, which produces a tiny voltage. The ESP32 reads that voltage as a number from 0 to 4095.
- One pole of the magnet pushes the voltage up, the other pole pushes it down. Flipping the magnet over flips the direction. That's why we measure distance from baseline rather than just "high" or "low".
- The 4-digit display shows the raw "strength" number so you can watch it climb as you get closer. Great for the kid - it's a literal number going up.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer alongside the LED for a metal-detector beep.
- The sketch already auto-calibrates the baseline on startup - try holding the magnet *near* the sensor at power-on and see how that messes things up. Good lesson in why calibration matters.
- Make it wireless: post each "find" to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is alive.
- Swap the single LED for a strip and light up more LEDs the closer you get (Cylon eyes).

## Why this is interesting

It's a sensor that detects something humans literally cannot perceive. Andy's son can hide the magnet under a book, in a cushion, behind a wall, and the ESP32 will still find it. That moment of "wait, it can see through stuff?" is the hook. It also teaches the analog-to-digital pipeline (real world -> voltage -> number -> behaviour) which is the foundation of basically every interesting sensor project that comes later.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED)
- 1x Soil Moisture Sensor (the two-prong probe + small comparator board; we only use the analog "AO" pin)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (the little blue/white screen; talks over 2 wires)
- 1x LED 5mm Red (the "thirsty" warning blinker) - the legs plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed
- 1x Resistor 220R (current limit for the red LED - never wire an LED straight to a GPIO) - leads plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (no soldering - everything plugs in)
- Jumper wires M-M (for the OLED and sensor connections - not for the LED itself)

## Wiring notes

Power rails first:

- XIAO **3V3** pin -> breadboard red (+) rail
- XIAO **GND** pin -> breadboard blue (-) rail

OLED (I2C, 4 wires - it shares the same 2 data lines no matter how many I2C things you add later):

- OLED **VCC** -> red rail (3.3V)
- OLED **GND** -> blue rail
- OLED **SDA** -> XIAO **D4** (GPIO 6, the default SDA on XIAO ESP32-C3)
- OLED **SCL** -> XIAO **D5** (GPIO 7, the default SCL on XIAO ESP32-C3)

Most 0.96" SSD1306 modules answer at I2C address **0x3C**, but a meaningful minority ship at **0x3D** (sometimes selectable by a resistor jumper on the back of the board). The sketch tries 0x3C first, then 0x3D, and prints which one worked over Serial - so you don't have to guess.

Soil sensor (analog - we read a voltage that changes with moisture):

- Sensor **VCC** -> XIAO **D2** (GPIO 4) - **not** the 3.3V rail. The sketch turns this pin on for ~10 ms around each reading and off in between. Continuously powering a resistive probe electrolyses the metal prongs and they corrode in weeks; gating the supply slows that down dramatically.
- Sensor **GND** -> blue rail
- Sensor **AO** -> XIAO **D0** (GPIO 2, an ADC-capable pin)
- The sensor's **DO** pin is left disconnected - that one is just an on/off threshold and we want the smooth analog value instead.
- Most common 4-pin LM393 boards happily accept 3.3V on VCC, which is what D2 supplies. A rare variant has an on-board 3-pin regulator and insists on 5V - if your board's silkscreen says "5V only", wire VCC to the XIAO's **5V** pin instead and accept the corrosion trade-off (or use a transistor to gate the 5V line).

Red LED (active-high - "HIGH = on"):

- XIAO **D1** (GPIO 3) -> one leg of the 220R resistor
- Other leg of the 220R -> long leg (anode, +) of the red LED
- Short leg (cathode, -) of the LED -> blue rail (GND)
- The LED legs and the resistor leads plug straight into the breadboard tie-points. No jumper wires for this part.

Sanity check before plugging in USB: LED short leg goes to GND, and there is exactly one resistor in series with the LED.

## Talking points

- Soil sensors work by measuring how easily electricity flows between the two prongs. Wet soil conducts; dry soil resists. The little board on the sensor converts that into a voltage on the AO pin. On the most common (LM393) boards a wet probe gives a **low** number and a dry probe gives a **high** number, but a few clones (and most capacitive replacements) flip that. The code has a `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` flag at the top - watch the Serial Monitor while you dunk the probe in water vs. hold it in air, and flip the flag if the relationship is reversed. The thresholds below it stay readable either way.
- The ESP32-C3 ADC turns that voltage into a number between **0 and 4095** (12 bits). We map "raw number" -> "happiness" with two thresholds.
- I2C is wonderful: SDA + SCL + power, and you can chain more sensors on the same two wires later (each with a unique address). Each device has its own address - that's why we needed to find the OLED at 0x3C or 0x3D.
- The face is drawn with three primitives: two filled circles for eyes, and either the bottom half of a circle (smile), a straight line (sleepy), or the top half of a circle plus two tear drops (crying). The "half a circle" trick uses `drawCircleHelper`, which is Adafruit_GFX's quadrant-selectable arc - cheaper than drawing a full circle and clipping.
- The LED only blinks when truly thirsty. A solid LED would be annoying; blinking screams "do something" without being constant.

## Things to change once it works

- **Calibrate the thresholds.** The defaults in the sketch are a starting guess. Hold the probe in air -> note the number printed to Serial; that's your "very dry". Stick it in a glass of water -> note that number; that's "very wet". Pick thresholds about a third and two-thirds of the way between. (And confirm which end is which - that's what `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` is for.)
- Plant the probe to the depth shown on the prongs (about 4 cm). Deeper isn't better - the metal contacts must stay above the water line of the pot's drainage saucer.
- Swap to a **capacitive** soil sensor when the resistive prongs corrode (gated power buys you weeks-to-months instead of weeks, but capacitive probes don't corrode at all). Same wiring, just better hardware - and remember to recheck `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW`, capacitive boards often invert.
- Add a buzzer on another GPIO for an audible "feed me" chirp once a day instead of just the LED.
- Have the XIAO publish moisture to MQTT once the Orange Pi is online, so the plant's mood appears on a phone dashboard.
- Add a small smoothing average (e.g. 10 readings) so a single noisy sample doesn't flip the face.

## Why this is interesting

It turns an invisible thing (soil moisture) into something a 10-year-old can read at a glance. There's a real, immediate consequence: water the plant and the face changes. It's also a clean introduction to the two most useful sensor categories - **analog** (a voltage you read with `analogRead`) and **I2C** (a digital bus you talk to with a library) - in the same small project, plus one quietly important trick (gating sensor power from a GPIO) that the same beginner can reuse on every battery-or-corrosion-sensitive sensor they meet next.

projects.name: Earthquake Cam
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (5V in). The ESP32's VIN pin re-exposes that 5V to power the MAX7219 matrix; the ESP32's onboard 3V3 regulator powers the SW-420 sensor and drives the GPIO logic.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain)
- 1x SW-420 vibration switch module (the "earthquake" sensor)
- 1x 8x8 LED matrix with MAX7219 driver board (the display)
- 1x yellow LED (the warning lamp that lights while a quake is being measured)
- 1x 220 ohm resistor (current-limit for the yellow LED)
- 1x breadboard, ~12 DuPont jumpers
- 1x USB cable (laptop to ESP32; this is also where the 5V for the matrix comes from)

## Wiring notes

Two power rails this time, not one. Bring the ESP32's `3V3` pin to one red breadboard strip, and the ESP32's `VIN` pin (which is the USB 5V passing through the board) to a *separate* red strip. Tie `GND` to the blue strip - both rails share ground.

- **8x8 LED matrix (MAX7219):** `VCC` to the **5V / VIN** rail, NOT 3V3. The MAX7219 datasheet wants 4.0 to 5.5 V; running it on 3.3 V is folk wisdom and can brown out the ESP32's onboard regulator when the panel lights up. `GND` to GND. `DIN` to `GPIO 23` (MOSI), `CS` to `GPIO 5`, `CLK` to `GPIO 18` (SCK). The MAX7219 reads anything above ~2 V as HIGH, so the ESP32's 3.3 V logic signals drive it fine directly.
- **SW-420 module:** `VCC` to **3V3**, `GND` to GND, `DO` (digital out) to ESP32 `GPIO 27`. The little blue trim-pot on the module sets the trigger threshold - if it triggers constantly even when still, turn that pot clockwise until the on-board "trigger" LED only blinks when you actually tap the board.
- **Yellow LED:** long leg (anode) through the 220 ohm resistor to `GPIO 26`. Short leg (cathode) to GND. The resistor stops the LED from burning out.
- Keep the SW-420 mounted firmly on the breadboard - if it dangles on jumper wires, the wires themselves will jiggle and trigger false quakes.

## Safety notes

Nothing in this build runs above 5 V, so the mains-safety warnings that apply to the 2-channel relay project explicitly do NOT apply here. The only real hazards are: (a) backwards LED polarity will simply not light, no damage; (b) shorting 5V to GND on the breadboard will trip the laptop's USB port protection but not hurt the ESP32. Unplug USB before re-wiring anything.

## Talking points

- The SW-420 isn't really a "sensor" in the analog sense - it's a tiny spring around a pin that briefly closes a circuit when shaken. So we don't measure shake *strength*, we count shake *pulses* per unit time. Lots of pulses in 10 seconds = bigger quake.
- We use a hardware *interrupt* on the sensor pin. Interrupts let the chip drop whatever it's doing the instant a pulse arrives and bump a counter. That way we never miss a bump even while the matrix is busy drawing. The interrupt is armed only *after* the boot animation, so bumps during startup don't trick the board into thinking a quake started before you arrived.
- The bar graph is drawn column by column. Eight columns, eight "Richter" levels. Each level also gets a label that scrolls across afterwards using a small built-in font.
- 25 ms debounce: a single physical tap can ring the spring several times within a few milliseconds. We ignore extra pulses inside a 25 ms window so one tap counts as one bump.
- We deliberately stick to the low-level `MD_MAX72XX` library and write the scrolling text by hand instead of mixing in the higher-level `MD_Parola`. Mixing the two on the same panel can cause one library's internal buffer to overwrite the other's drawing - confusing to debug as a beginner.

## Things to change once it works

- If the matrix shows garbled, scrambled, mirrored or upside-down output, change `HARDWARE_TYPE` in the code. Try `GENERIC_HW`, then `PAROLA_HW`, then `ICSTATION_HW` until it looks right. This is the single biggest gotcha with cheap matrix modules.
- Lower the SW-420 sensitivity pot (turn clockwise) to make it harder to trigger - then you have to really thump the table to reach "GODZILLA".
- Add a second LED (red) for "BIG ONE" and above, so the warning lamp escalates.
- Replace the verdict labels with funny ones aimed at Andy's son.
- Once the Orange Pi is online, publish each quake's count + level to MQTT so the Pi can keep a high-score table.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project that *reacts* to the physical world instead of timing or button presses. It teaches three new ideas at once: reading a digital sensor through an interrupt, accumulating events over a time window, and driving a real graphical display (the 8x8 matrix) with a library. And the feedback loop is irresistible: you hit the table, the matrix lights up, you hit it harder, it scrolls "GODZILLA". Hard to put down.

<![CDATA[// Earthquake Cam
// ESP32 NodeMCU + SW-420 vibration switch + MAX7219 8x8 LED matrix + warning LED.
// On any shake, count the bumps over a 10-second window and show a Richter-style
// bar graph + a verdict label ("MOUSE FART" ... "GODZILLA").
//
// Library needed (install once in Arduino IDE Library Manager):
//   "MD_MAX72XX"  by majicDesigns
//
// Arduino IDE board:  ESP32 Arduino > ESP32 Dev Module
//
// POWER NOTE: the matrix VCC goes to the ESP32's 5V / VIN pin (USB-powered),
// NOT to 3V3. The MAX7219 datasheet wants 4.0 to 5.5 V. The ESP32 GPIO logic
// is 3.3 V but the MAX7219 reads anything above ~2 V as HIGH, so direct
// connections from GPIO to DIN/CS/CLK work fine.

#include <SPI.h>
#include <MD_MAX72xx.h>

// ---- Pin map (matches the wiring diagram) ----
const int PIN_SW420    = 27;   // SW-420 digital OUT
const int PIN_LED_WARN = 26;   // Yellow warning LED through 220R
const int PIN_MATRIX_CS = 5;   // MAX7219 CS / LOAD
// MOSI = GPIO 23, SCK = GPIO 18 (hardware SPI defaults on ESP32)

// ---- Matrix config ----
// If the display looks garbled, scrambled, mirrored, or upside-down,
// try the OTHER values below in order. This single line is the #1
// thing that varies between cheap 8x8 modules.
//   FC16_HW       <- most common on "FC-16" red modules (try first)
//   GENERIC_HW    <- many no-name eBay/Aliexpress modules
//   PAROLA_HW     <- original Parola-branded boards
//   ICSTATION_HW  <- IcStation-branded boards
#define HARDWARE_TYPE MD_MAX72XX::FC16_HW
#define MAX_DEVICES   1
MD_MAX72XX matrix = MD_MAX72XX(HARDWARE_TYPE, PIN_MATRIX_CS, MAX_DEVICES);

// ---- Event counting ----
const unsigned long WINDOW_MS   = 10000UL;   // 10 second measuring window
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 25UL;      // ignore re-triggers inside this gap

volatile unsigned long lastPulseMs = 0;
volatile unsigned int  pulseCount  = 0;

void IRAM_ATTR onShake() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastPulseMs >= DEBOUNCE_MS) {
    lastPulseMs = now;
    pulseCount++;
  }
}

// Map a count to a 1..8 "Richter" level for the bar graph.
int countToLevel(unsigned int count) {
  if (count <= 1)   return 1;
  if (count <= 3)   return 2;
  if (count <= 6)   return 3;
  if (count <= 10)  return 4;
  if (count <= 18)  return 5;
  if (count <= 30)  return 6;
  if (count <= 50)  return 7;
  return 8;
}

const char* levelToVerdict(int level) {
  switch (level) {
    case 1: return "MOUSE FART";
    case 2: return "TIPTOE";
    case 3: return "BUMP";
    case 4: return "STOMP";
    case 5: return "TRUCK";
    case 6: return "QUAKE";
    case 7: return "BIG ONE";
    default: return "GODZILLA";
  }
}

// ---- Tiny 5x7 font for the scrolling verdict (uppercase + space only). ----
// Each glyph is 5 columns wide; bit 0 = top row, bit 6 = bottom row.
struct Glyph { char c; uint8_t col[5]; };
const Glyph FONT[] = {
  {' ', {0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00}},
  {'A', {0x7E,0x11,0x11,0x11,0x7E}},
  {'B', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x36}},
  {'C', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x22}},
  {'D', {0x7F,0x41,0x41,0x22,0x1C}},
  {'E', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x41}},
  {'F', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x01}},
  {'G', {0x3E,0x41,0x49,0x49,0x7A}},
  {'H', {0x7F,0x08,0x08,0x08,0x7F}},
  {'I', {0x00,0x41,0x7F,0x41,0x00}},
  {'K', {0x7F,0x08,0x14,0x22,0x41}},
  {'L', {0x7F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x40}},
  {'M', {0x7F,0x02,0x0C,0x02,0x7F}},
  {'N', {0x7F,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x7F}},
  {'O', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x3E}},
  {'P', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x06}},
  {'Q', {0x3E,0x41,0x51,0x21,0x5E}},
  {'R', {0x7F,0x09,0x19,0x29,0x46}},
  {'S', {0x46,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x31}},
  {'T', {0x01,0x01,0x7F,0x01,0x01}},
  {'U', {0x3F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x3F}},
  {'Z', {0x61,0x51,0x49,0x45,0x43}},
};

const uint8_t* glyphFor(char c) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(FONT)/sizeof(FONT[0]); i++) {
    if (FONT[i].c == c) return FONT[i].col;
  }
  return FONT[0].col;  // space if missing
}

// Build a column buffer for a whole message: 5 cols per glyph + 1 blank gap,
// plus 8 blank cols of padding at the start and end so it scrolls cleanly.
size_t buildMessage(const char* msg, uint8_t* out, size_t outCap) {
  size_t n = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  for (const char* p = msg; *p && n + 6 < outCap; p++) {
    const uint8_t* g = glyphFor(*p);
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) out[n++] = g[i];
    out[n++] = 0x00;
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  return n;
}

// Scroll a 1..N column buffer across the 8-column matrix, ~60 ms per step.
void scrollColumns(const uint8_t* cols, size_t n) {
  for (size_t start = 0; start + 8 <= n; start++) {
    matrix.clear();
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
      matrix.setColumn(7 - c, cols[start + c]);
    }
    delay(60);
  }
}

// Draw a vertical bar graph: `level` columns lit from the left, full height.
void drawBar(int level) {
  matrix.clear();
  for (int col = 0; col < level && col < 8; col++) {
    matrix.setColumn(col, 0xFF);   // light all 8 rows in this column
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(200);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println(F("Earthquake Cam booting..."));

  pinMode(PIN_LED_WARN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);

  // INPUT_PULLUP is defensive: most SW-420 breakouts have an LM393 comparator
  // with its own pull-up, but bare-module variants without the comparator
  // need the MCU to pull the line high. Adding INPUT_PULLUP is harmless on
  // the comparator boards and saves the bare ones.
  pinMode(PIN_SW420, INPUT_PULLUP);

  matrix.begin();
  matrix.control(MD_MAX72XX::INTENSITY, 4);   // 0..15
  matrix.clear();

  // Friendly boot "READY" scroll BEFORE we arm the interrupt, so that bumps
  // landing during setup don't leave a stale pulseCount > 0 when loop() starts.
  uint8_t buf[64];
  size_t n = buildMessage("READY", buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // Now arm the shake interrupt and zero the counter for a clean start.
  pulseCount  = 0;
  lastPulseMs = 0;
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(PIN_SW420), onShake, FALLING);

  Serial.println(F("Ready. Bump the sensor to start a measurement."));
}

void loop() {
  // Idle: wait for the very first pulse to open a measurement window.
  if (pulseCount == 0) {
    delay(10);
    return;
  }

  // A shake just happened. Light the warning LED and count for WINDOW_MS.
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, HIGH);
  unsigned long windowStart = millis();
  Serial.println(F("Quake window opened."));

  // Show a small "live" tick on the matrix while counting (column 0 blinks).
  bool tick = false;
  unsigned long lastTickMs = 0;
  while (millis() - windowStart < WINDOW_MS) {
    if (millis() - lastTickMs >= 250) {
      lastTickMs = millis();
      tick = !tick;
      matrix.clear();
      matrix.setColumn(0, tick ? 0x18 : 0x00);  // middle two rows blink
    }
    delay(5);
  }

  // Snapshot the count, then reset for the next quake.
  noInterrupts();
  unsigned int finalCount = pulseCount;
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();

  int level = countToLevel(finalCount);
  const char* verdict = levelToVerdict(level);

  Serial.print(F("Pulses in window: "));
  Serial.print(finalCount);
  Serial.print(F("  ->  level "));
  Serial.print(level);
  Serial.print(F("  ("));
  Serial.print(verdict);
  Serial.println(F(")"));

  // Show the bar graph for 2 seconds...
  drawBar(level);
  delay(2000);

  // ...then scroll the verdict label across the matrix once.
  matrix.clear();
  uint8_t buf[96];
  size_t n = buildMessage(verdict, buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // All done. Turn the warning lamp off and go back to idle.
  // Drain any pulses that arrived during the display so we don't immediately
  // re-trigger from the user celebrating their GODZILLA score.
  noInterrupts();
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);
  Serial.println(F("Quake window closed. Waiting for the next bump."));
}

projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via the board's USB port, 3.3V on the GPIO header)
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - runs the state machine and the randomizer)
- 1x Red, 1x Yellow, 1x Green, 1x Blue 5mm LED (the four "Simon" pads)
- 4x 220 ohm resistors (one in series with each LED so the LED does not burn out)
- 4x tactile push-buttons (one under each LED)
- 1x breadboard, ~18 DuPont jumpers
- USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (also how power gets in)

No external pull-up resistors are needed because every button GPIO chosen here (32, 33, 13, 19) supports the ESP32's internal pull-up.

## Wiring notes

LEDs (one per color, repeat the same pattern four times):

- ESP32 GPIO -> 220 ohm resistor -> LED anode (long leg)
- LED cathode (short leg, with the flat side) -> breadboard GND rail
- GPIOs used: Red = 25, Yellow = 26, Green = 27, Blue = 14

Buttons (also one per color):

- One leg of the button -> an ESP32 GPIO
- The opposite leg -> breadboard GND rail
- No external pull-up resistor needed - the sketch turns on the ESP32's internal pull-up, so the GPIO sits HIGH at rest and reads LOW when pressed
- GPIOs used: Red = 32, Yellow = 33, Green = 13, Blue = 19

Power rails:

- ESP32 `GND` -> breadboard "-" rail. All four LED cathodes and all four button ground legs come here.
- The `3V3` pin is not needed for this project - every GPIO already provides its own pull-up internally.

Pin notes (worth knowing):

- GPIO 34, 35, 36, 39 are INPUT-ONLY on the ESP32 and have NO internal pull-up. They look tempting because there are four of them, but a button wired only between an input-only pin and GND will float when released and give random readings. If you ever want to use one anyway, add an external 10 k ohm pull-up resistor from the pin to 3V3.
- Avoid GPIO 0, 12, 15 for buttons - they are boot-strapping pins and can stop the board from starting if held LOW or HIGH at power-on.
- GPIO 2 is the on-board blue user LED on this board. Do not reuse it for a button - the LED and the button would fight each other.

## Talking points

- The "memory" of the game is just an array of numbers. Each new round appends a fresh random value (0-3) and replays the whole array from the start.
- Debouncing: when you press a tactile button the metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, so the GPIO sees several rapid LOW/HIGH/LOW transitions. The sketch reads the pin, waits a tiny moment (`DEBOUNCE_MS`), and reads again to confirm.
- `INPUT_PULLUP` flips your intuition: pressed = LOW, not pressed = HIGH. That is because the internal resistor pulls the pin to 3.3 V by default, and the button shorts it to GND when you press it. This is why pin choice matters - GPIOs without a built-in pull-up have nothing to flip back to HIGH.
- The speed-up: every successful round trims the gap between LED flashes. That is the difficulty curve, baked into one variable.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a tiny passive buzzer on another GPIO and play a different tone per colour (real Simon does this).
- Save the high score to flash with the `Preferences` library so it survives a reset.
- Add a 2-player mode: alternate who has to repeat the sequence.
- Replace the four discrete LEDs with a single WS2812 strip and use colour directly.
- Make it WiFi-aware and POST the high score to the Orange Pi hub (once the Pi is online).

## Why this is interesting

Pure software project - no sensors, no analog, no I2C. Everything interesting happens in the code: the array, the random call, the loop that plays it back, the loop that reads the player. It is the perfect introduction to a finite state machine (SHOW_SEQUENCE -> WAIT_FOR_PLAYER -> CHECK -> WIN/LOSE) without any new electrical concepts. And the game is genuinely fun, which keeps a 10-year-old engaged long enough to ask "but how does it remember?" - which is exactly the question worth answering.

projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via USB, the onboard regulator makes 3.3V for the chip; no external parts so nothing else needs feeding).
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the entire project - nothing else needed)
- 1x USB-C cable from your laptop

That is the whole shopping list. This version of the project was deliberately re-scoped so it can be built with **only the hardware already in Andy's kit**. An earlier draft used a TM1637 4-digit display, an SSD1306 OLED, two tactile push-buttons, a breadboard, and jumpers - none of which are in the kit yet. When those parts arrive, see "Things to change once it works" for the upgrade path.

## Wiring notes

There is no wiring. Plug the USB-C cable from your laptop into the ESP32. That is it. The two pieces of "hardware UI" we use are both already on the board:

- **BOOT button** (next to the USB-C jack). It is wired to GPIO 0 with a built-in pull-up. Pressed = LOW, released = HIGH. We use it as our one user button.
- **Built-in blue LED** on GPIO 2 (the small LED next to the WiFi shield, not the red power LED). It blinks once a second while the stopwatch is running and is off when stopped, so you can see the state at a glance without looking at the screen.

The "display" is the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Open it with `Tools > Serial Monitor` (or Ctrl+Shift+M) after upload.

**Do not press the EN button while timing** - EN is a hardware reset, it reboots the chip and you lose the run. Only BOOT is safe to press.

## Talking points

- **Why `millis()` instead of `delay()`.** `delay(1000)` would freeze the chip for a whole second, during which it cannot read the button or update the LED. `millis()` just asks "how many milliseconds since boot?" without stopping anything, so the same `loop()` can poll the button, blink the LED, and print the time all at once.
- **One button, three actions, via a small state machine.** A short tap (< 600 ms) toggles start/stop. A long press (>= 600 ms while held) records a lap if running, or resets everything if stopped. The function `readButton()` measures how long the button was held and reports a `SHORT_PRESS` or `LONG_PRESS` event. The `loop()` then decides what that event means based on whether the stopwatch is currently running. That separation - "low-level: was it short or long?" vs. "high-level: what does that mean right now?" - is the core idea of a state machine, and it shows up in almost every embedded project later.
- **Active-LOW buttons.** When BOOT is *pressed*, GPIO 0 reads `LOW` (0V), not `HIGH`. That is because the pin is pulled up to 3.3V by default, and pressing the button shorts it to ground. This is the single most common thing beginners get backwards, so it is worth re-reading: pressed = LOW.
- **Debouncing.** Real metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when you press them - the pin flickers HIGH/LOW/HIGH/LOW before settling. `readButton()` ignores any change that happens within 25 ms of the last change, which filters that out so one press is one event.
- **Why GPIO 0 is "free" to use as a button at runtime.** GPIO 0 is sampled at *boot* to decide between normal-run mode and flash-upload mode (that is why you sometimes have to hold BOOT during upload). Once the sketch is running, GPIO 0 is just a regular input - so we can re-use the BOOT button as our user button without any extra hardware.
- **Why the built-in LED is GPIO 2 on this board.** A few clones put it on GPIO 5 or GPIO 22 instead. If the LED never blinks, change `PIN_LED` to 5 or 22 - the rest of the sketch will still work.

## Things to change once it works

- **Upgrade to a real display.** When a TM1637 4-digit display arrives, replace the `Serial.print` calls in `showBigTime()` with `TM1637Display::setSegments()` and keep everything else identical. Add an SSD1306 OLED for the lap list. (That is the original "big stopwatch face + scrolling lap history" project, deferred until the parts are in hand.)
- **Add a buzzer.** When the relay board is wired up to switch a piezo, beep once per lap so Andy's son can time himself without watching the screen.
- **Persist the best-ever lap.** Use the `Preferences` library to save `bestLapMs` to ESP32 flash so it survives a power cycle.
- **Push laps over WiFi.** Once the Orange Pi One is booted and running Mosquitto, publish each lap time over MQTT to the Pi for plotting in Grafana. That makes this the first project that talks to the future hub.
- **Increase `MAX_LAPS`** from 20 to 100 - the ESP32 has plenty of RAM.

## Why this is interesting

This project teaches the three skills that come up in nearly every later IoT project - **non-blocking timing with `millis()`**, **debounced button input with a state machine**, and **storing a short history in a fixed-size array** - using only the hardware that is already on the desk. There is nothing to wire wrong and nothing to fry. By the end, the same `loop()` that times your son's 100-metre sprint will be a working template for the next dozen projects, where the "display" becomes a TM1637 or an OLED and the "button" becomes any other GPIO input.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - hosts the web page and watches the button)
- 1x push button (the doorbell itself)
- 1x breadboard (holds the button without soldering)
- 4x DuPont jumper wires (one to GPIO 4, one to GND, two spare)
- 1x USB cable (powers the ESP32 from a laptop or USB wall charger)

No resistor is needed for the button: we turn on the ESP32's internal pull-up resistor in code (`INPUT_PULLUP`). The LED that lights up on each press is the blue one already built into the NodeMCU board, so it has its own resistor on the PCB.

## Wiring notes

The button has 4 legs but they are wired in pairs internally. Sit the button across the breadboard's centre gap. Use diagonally opposite legs - that way you can't accidentally pick two legs that are already shorted together.

- One leg of the button -> ESP32 `GPIO 4`
- Diagonally opposite leg of the button -> ESP32 `GND`

That's all the wiring. When the button is open, GPIO 4 reads HIGH (pulled up internally to 3.3V). When pressed, GPIO 4 is shorted to GND and reads LOW. The code watches for that transition.

Power comes from the USB cable on the ESP32 - no separate power supply, no battery, nothing to plug into mains.

## Talking points

- The button is just a switch. No "smartness" in it. The ESP32 is what turns "switch closed" into "tell every phone in the house".
- The web page doesn't get pushed to; it asks the ESP32 every second "has the count gone up?". That's called polling. It's the simplest approach that works on every phone browser without extra libraries.
- We count rings instead of just storing "is ringing". A counter means two phones loading the page at slightly different times still both notice the same press.
- Debouncing: a physical button's metal contacts bounce when they touch, so one press can look like 3-5 presses electrically. The 400 ms timer in the code ignores those echoes.

## Things to change once it works

- Make the page beep or vibrate the phone (a tiny bit of Web Audio API or `navigator.vibrate`).
- Add a mDNS name (`ESP32.local`) so you don't have to memorise the IP.
- Push instead of poll: switch to Server-Sent Events (`/events` endpoint) so the page updates instantly with no 1-second lag.
- Log the last 10 rings with timestamps so you can see who rang while you were out.
- Move from the breadboard button to a real doorbell button by the front door (still 2 wires).

## Why this is interesting

This is the smallest possible "real" IoT loop: a thing in the physical world (a button) makes a thing on a screen change (a web page), with nothing in between except WiFi. Andy gets to feel the whole shape of an event-driven system in one afternoon - sensor -> microcontroller -> network -> UI - and his son gets immediate, obvious feedback (Dad's phone goes "Ding!" when he pushes the button). It's also the natural feeder project for the Orange Pi hub later: replace the polling page with an MQTT publish and the doorbell becomes one of many sensors on the home bus.
