projects.description:
## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brains and web server)
- 2-ch Songle relay board (only channel 1 is used here)
- 12V LED strip, short piece, or any 12V low-voltage lamp
- 12V DC power supply for the LED strip (separate from the ESP32 USB power)
- Breadboard (holds the ESP32 only)
- DuPont jumper wires (M-F from ESP32 header to relay header, M-M for the 12V load side)
- USB-A to USB-C cable (the NodeMCU-32S has a USB-C connector)

Heads-up: only the ESP32 and the relay board are confirmed on hand from the kit list in CLAUDE.md. The 12V strip, 12V supply, breadboard, jumpers, and USB-C cable are not listed there. Confirm these are actually in the box before starting, or we will be stuck halfway through wiring.

## Wiring notes

Two power worlds meet in this project. Keep them straight.

ESP32 side (5V from USB):

- ESP32 `5V` pin -> relay header `VCC`
- ESP32 `GND` -> relay header `GND`
- ESP32 `GPIO 26` -> relay header `IN1`

The breadboard is just a perch for the ESP32 and a convenient place to start the three jumpers that run to the relay header. The relay board already has its own logic pin header, so nothing else is wired on the breadboard rails.

The relay's JDVcc jumper stays in its default position (bridged to Vcc), so the relay coil is powered from the ESP32's 5V USB rail. This is the simplest wiring and fine for a small DC load.

12V side (the load being switched):

- 12V supply `+` -> relay channel 1 `COM` screw terminal
- Relay channel 1 `NO` screw terminal -> LED strip `+`
- LED strip `-` -> 12V supply `-`

The 12V supply ground does NOT need to touch the ESP32 ground. That is the whole point of the relay: the high-side wire is broken and remade by a mechanical contact, with no electrical connection back to the ESP32.

Active-LOW gotcha: the Songle board energizes the coil when IN1 is pulled LOW. The code drives the pin HIGH before calling `pinMode(..., OUTPUT)` so the relay does not click ON during boot.

3.3V trigger caveat (per CLAUDE.md, `Relay_2CH_Songle/` section): most Songle clones will trigger fine off a 3.3V ESP32 GPIO because the optocoupler LED only needs a small forward current. A few stubborn ones really do want a 5V swing - if relay 1 clicks unreliably, only sometimes, or only after the board warms up, that is the first thing to suspect. Workaround is a tiny NPN transistor or a level-shifter feeding IN1; ask before reaching for those, it is rarely needed.

## Talking points

- The relay is a remote-controlled light switch. The ESP32 cannot handle 12V directly, so it tells a tiny electromagnet (the relay coil) to physically push two metal contacts together.
- Hear the click? That is the contacts closing. That click is also why you should not switch a relay thousands of times a second.
- The web page is just HTML the ESP32 builds as a string and sends back when your phone asks for it. The big button is a link to `/on` or `/off`. The ESP32 sees the request, flips the pin, and redirects you back to `/` so the page updates.
- `digitalWrite(pin, LOW)` turns the light ON here. That feels backwards, and it is. Most opto-isolated relay boards use "low-level trigger".
- Because the button is a plain link with a 303 redirect, every tap reloads the whole page. That is fine for learning, but it will feel a little sluggish on a phone - half a second of white flash between taps. The first upgrade below fixes that.

## Things to change once it works

- Replace the link-style buttons with a `fetch()` call so the page does not fully reload on every tap (the current 303-redirect design forces a full reload, which is why it feels slow).
- Add channel 2 with a second button for a second light.
- Add a `/status` endpoint that returns JSON so a phone app or Home Assistant can poll it.
- Once the Orange Pi hub is up, switch from "web page" to MQTT: ESP32 subscribes to `home/garage/light/set`, publishes state to `home/garage/light/state`.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project where a tap on a phone moves a thing in the real world. Everything before this was the ESP32 talking to its own onboard LED. Now there is a 12V load, a separate power supply, and a mechanical click you can hear from across the room. That click is the bridge from "blinky tutorials" to "actually controlling the house".

projects.name: WiFi Signal Strength Meter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a power bank (user-supplied) to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S USB-C port (5V). The board powers the OLED off its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
## Parts list

From Andy's inventory:

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the "brain" - reads WiFi signal strength and drives the screen)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - SSD1306, 128x64 monochrome (the little screen that shows the bar graph)
- 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) (for tidy wiring without solder)
- 4x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc (we use 4 of the 40-pack: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL between ESP32 and OLED)

Not in the inventory - grab from around the house:

- USB power bank (any 5V "phone charger" pack with a USB output)
- USB-C cable to go from the power bank to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S's USB-C port

These two are treated as user-supplied because they aren't catalogued in the electronics stock - any spare phone-charging gear will do.

## Wiring notes

The OLED is an "I2C" device, which means it talks to the ESP32 over just two signal wires plus power and ground - four wires total. I2C is great because you can hang several different I2C devices off the same two pins later without needing more GPIO.

- OLED `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3` pin (the OLED is happy with 3.3V; do NOT use the 5V pin or the screen can be damaged)
- OLED `GND` -> ESP32 `GND` pin
- OLED `SDA` -> ESP32 `GPIO 21` (the default I2C data pin on the ESP32)
- OLED `SCL` -> ESP32 `GPIO 22` (the default I2C clock pin on the ESP32)

Plug both modules into the breadboard so nothing is dangling, then run the four jumpers between them. When you finish testing on the laptop, unplug the USB cable and move it to the power bank - everything keeps running because the ESP32 is happy with any 5V USB source.

Before uploading: open `WiFiRSSIMeter.ino` and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real GeeFam WiFi password. Per the project convention, credentials live inside the sketch (not in any CLAUDE.md or commit).

## Talking points

- **RSSI** (Received Signal Strength Indicator) is just a number in dBm that the WiFi chip reports for the access point it's connected to. -30 dBm is "I'm sitting on the router", -90 dBm is "I can barely hear it". -67 dBm or better is fine for streaming video, worse than -75 dBm is where things get flaky.
- The bar graph is just a filled rectangle whose width is mapped from the RSSI range onto the screen width. It's the same idea as a volume bar in any music app.
- "I2C" uses only two signal wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and an address to pick which device on the bus to talk to. The OLED's address is almost always `0x3C`.
- Because the ESP32 reconnects to WiFi automatically, you can keep walking around even if the signal drops out briefly - the meter will recover on its own.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a peak-hold marker: a thin vertical line that remembers the strongest reading you've seen in this room.
- Show the SSID name and the IP address as small text above the bar, so the kids can confirm which network they're measuring.
- Log readings to SD or send them over MQTT to the (future) Orange Pi hub so you can make a heat-map of the house.
- Add a buzzer that beeps faster when signal gets weaker - a "Geiger counter" mode for finding the strongest spot.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project here that does something genuinely useful around the house: it answers the real question "why is the WiFi bad in the back bedroom?". It also introduces two big concepts in one go - reading a real-world radio measurement (RSSI) and driving a display over I2C - without needing any sensors or extra parts beyond a single screen. Once the OLED is working, every future project that needs a tiny readout (temperature, sensor values, MQTT status from the Pi) reuses exactly the same wiring and code pattern.

projects.name: Distance-Triggered Treat Dispenser
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (or laptop port) into the ESP32 NodeMCU; VIN/5V feeds the HC-SR04 and SG90 with a 470 uF cap across the servo rail, and the HC-SR04 ECHO line is divided 1k/2k down to 3.3V before reaching the ESP32 GPIO.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain - reads sensor, drives servo, updates display)
- HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance module (looks straight up for your hand)
- SG90 micro-servo (rotates the cardboard disk that drops one M&M)
- TM1637 4-digit display (shows the running count of treats dispensed)
- 1k and 2k resistors (voltage divider on the HC-SR04 ECHO line - see Wiring notes)
- 470 uF electrolytic capacitor (across the servo's 5V/GND, prevents brownout resets)
- Breadboard + male-to-male DuPont jumpers
- USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (preferred) or a laptop port for power

You will also build a tiny cardboard chassis: a tube (like an empty toilet-roll tube) holds the M&Ms, a flat cardboard disk on the servo horn has one M&M-sized slot cut out of it. As the servo turns from 0 deg to 90 deg the slot lines up with a hole in the chute and exactly one M&M drops out. This is the fun part - it will probably take three tries to get the disk geometry right.

## Wiring notes

- The HC-SR04 needs 5V on Vcc and its ECHO pin outputs 5V logic. The ESP32's GPIOs are 3.3V (not 5V tolerant on the datasheet), so we drop ECHO with a simple 1k / 2k divider: ECHO -> 1k -> GPIO 18, and GPIO 18 -> 2k -> GND. That gives 5 V x 2k / (1k + 2k) = ~3.3 V at the GPIO. TRIG goes the other way (ESP32 out to sensor in) and a 3.3 V high is enough to trigger the HC-SR04, so no divider needed there.
- The SG90 servo also wants 5V. Both 5V devices share the ESP32's VIN/5V pin (which on the NodeMCU board comes straight from the USB connector). The servo can briefly draw 500-700 mA when it stalls, and that dip on the shared rail can reset the ESP32. We park a 470 uF electrolytic capacitor right across the servo's 5V and GND on the breadboard rail to absorb those dips. Mind the polarity: the striped leg is the negative side and goes to GND. Use a 5V/2A USB charger rather than a laptop port if you can.
- The TM1637 display is happy on 3.3V or 5V; we use 3.3V because the data lines are then natively at ESP32 logic level.
- All grounds tie together on the breadboard's blue rail. This is essential - if the sensor's ground floats, distance readings will be garbage.

## Talking points

- "What is an ultrasonic sensor?" It chirps a sound too high-pitched for us to hear, then times how long the echo takes to come back. Sound travels ~343 m/s, so the code multiplies microseconds by 0.0343 cm/us and divides by 2 (because the chirp goes there and back).
- "Why does it only dispense one M&M, not a stream?" Look at the `armed` variable. We disarm as soon as a hand is detected and only re-arm once the hand has moved back past 20 cm. That hysteresis pattern shows up everywhere in electronics - thermostats, button debouncing, you name it.
- "Why a slotted disk instead of just a flap?" A flap can let two M&Ms through if you're unlucky. A slot exactly one M&M deep is mechanically self-limiting - this is called a "rotary feeder" and is how real candy machines work.
- "Why two resistors on the ECHO wire?" The sensor speaks at 5 V but the ESP32 listens at 3.3 V. The two resistors form a divider that quietly drops the loud 5 V down to a polite 3.3 V before it reaches the chip - cheap insurance against frying a GPIO.
- "Why a fat capacitor next to the servo?" Motors are greedy in short bursts. The cap is a tiny local battery that hands current to the servo during those bursts so the ESP32 next door does not see its supply sag and reboot.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a tiny buzzer (active-high) that beeps once per dispense.
- Display the time-since-last-treat instead of the count, so you can compete with your son for "fastest reaction".
- Publish the count over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) so a Grafana dashboard tracks daily M&M consumption.
- Replace the cardboard disk with a 3D-printed one - same code, much more reliable feed.
- Add a long-press boot button check that resets the counter to zero.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project in the kit that combines a sensor (input), an actuator (output), and a display (feedback) into one closed loop. That is the basic shape of every IoT device. It also forces you to think about mechanical design as part of "the code working" - the firmware is the easy half, the cardboard is the hard half. That's a really useful lesson before moving on to the Orange Pi hub work where you'll be debugging across networks instead of across millimetres of cardboard.

projects.name: Mailbox-Opened Pinger
projects.power_supply: 18650 cell, charged by a TP4056 charge-only module; cell B+ goes straight to the XIAO BAT pad (3.7V, no boost stage), B- to XIAO GND
projects.description:
A battery-powered XIAO ESP32-C3 sits inside the mailbox, asleep almost all the time. When the mail carrier lifts the flap, a tilt switch closes, pulls a GPIO pin HIGH, and the C3 wakes from deep sleep. It connects to WiFi, fires off an HTTP ping, blinks the indoor LED, then goes back to sleep. With the boost stage removed and the 18650 wired straight to the XIAO's battery pad, a single cell should run the project for a long time - though see the honest battery-life note below.

## Parts list

- 1x XIAO ESP32-C3 (the sleeper)
- 1x bare 2-pin Angle Tilt Switch (a tube with a metal ball that bridges two contacts when tilted - no electronics inside)
- 1x 18650 cell + TP4056 charge-only module (power)
- 1x 100k resistor - external pull-down on the wake pin AND the R of an RC debounce filter
- 1x 100nF ceramic cap - the C of the same RC debounce filter
- 1x Blue LED + 1x 100R resistor (visible "I woke up" indicator)
- 1x Breadboard, ~8x M-M DuPont jumpers

## Wiring notes

**Power path (no boost stage - this matters for battery life):**

- USB-C into the TP4056's input only when you want to charge the cell.
- 18650 cell into the TP4056's B+ / B- pads.
- TP4056 OUT+ goes to the XIAO's BAT pad (on the underside of the board - Seeed exposes it specifically for this use case). OUT- goes to XIAO GND.
- The XIAO's own LDO runs directly from the 3.7V cell - no boost-to-5V-then-back-down-to-3.3V round trip, which was costing milliamps of quiescent current 24/7 in the earlier draft.

**Tilt switch wiring (bare 2-pin switch + external pull-down + RC debounce):**

- One leg of the tilt switch to 3V3 on the XIAO.
- Other leg to GPIO2 (D0) AND to one leg of the 100nF cap AND to one leg of the 100k resistor.
- Other leg of the 100nF cap to GND.
- Other leg of the 100k resistor to GND.

That little RC network does two jobs at once:
- The 100k pulls GPIO2 firmly LOW whenever the switch is open (including during deep sleep, when the chip's own internal pull-downs are off).
- The 100k + 100nF together form a low-pass filter with a ~10ms time constant, which absorbs the contact bounce of the ball rolling around in the tube.

**LED:**

- LED long leg (anode) to XIAO D1 (GPIO3) through the 100R resistor.
- LED short leg (cathode) to XIAO GND.
- (220R was too large here. Blue LEDs have a forward voltage around 3.0-3.2V, so on a 3.3V GPIO the resistor sees only ~0.1-0.3V of headroom. 100R gives a few mA of forward current - bright enough to see across the room. If yours still looks dim, a direct connection through a 47R will work too; the GPIO source limit (40 mA absolute max) is what protects it at that point.)

**Why GPIO2 specifically, and the strapping-pin warning:**

On the ESP32-C3, GPIO2 is one of the pins that can wake the chip from deep sleep via the GPIO wake source. It is ALSO a strapping pin: its level at the moment of reset/power-on selects boot mode. The design here is safe because the tilt switch idles OPEN (so the 100k pulls GPIO2 LOW = normal boot) when the mailbox flap is closed. If you ever wire / mount the switch so its idle position is CLOSED (GPIO2 HIGH at power-on), the chip can land in download mode on power-up and look bricked - so mount the switch so "flap closed" = "switch open".

## Talking points

- **Deep sleep is the headline feature.** A XIAO running normally pulls ~80 mA with WiFi on. In deep sleep the chip itself drops to roughly 40-150 microamps.
- **But "weeks to months" needs an honest asterisk.** The boost-converter round-trip in the earlier draft was leaking 1-10 mA all the time, which would have dominated the chip's own 43 uA and killed the cell in days. Going straight from the 18650 to the XIAO BAT pad removes that loss. The remaining drains are the TP4056 (~20 uA when idle, no USB plugged in), the chip itself in deep sleep (~40 uA), and the 100k pull-down (only conducts while the switch is closed). So the realistic budget is in the tens-of-microamps range - genuinely weeks of life - PROVIDED the tilt switch doesn't bounce back and forth all day. A single mail delivery that bounces 20 times is fine; a wind-rattled flap that wakes the chip every 30 seconds will flatten the cell in a day.
- **The C3 needs a different deep-sleep wake API than the classic ESP32.** The classic ESP32 has an `ext1` wake source that uses the RTC_IO peripheral, but the C3 doesn't have that peripheral, so `esp_sleep_enable_ext1_wakeup` won't work as expected. On the C3 you use `gpio_wakeup_enable()` plus `esp_deep_sleep_enable_gpio_wakeup()`, and you check `ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_GPIO` (not `_EXT1`) for the wake cause. This is one of those quiet behavior differences between ESP32 family members that the part name doesn't telegraph.
- **RTC_DATA_ATTR variables survive sleep.** The `bootCount` variable keeps its value across wake/sleep cycles because we put it in RTC memory, which stays powered. Regular variables get wiped.
- **Why a brief LED pulse before WiFi?** So even if WiFi is down, you still get a visible confirmation that the wake actually happened. Debugging "did it wake?" vs "did the ping fail?" separately is much easier than debugging both at once.

## Things to change once it works

1. **Replace the demo HTTP endpoint** with something real: a Home Assistant webhook, an IFTTT trigger, a Pushover/ntfy notification, or your own MQTT publish to the Orange Pi once it's booted.
2. **Measure actual battery life.** Add a divider to read the battery voltage on an ADC pin and include it in the ping payload. Then graph it over a week and see how the cell is really discharging.
3. **Weatherproof the enclosure.** A small project box with a cable gland for the tilt-switch leads. The XIAO and battery stay inside the house; only the switch goes in the mailbox.
4. **Add a second debounce layer in software** if mailbox flap wind-rattle turns out to be a problem - e.g., require the line to stay HIGH for 100ms before treating it as a real event, otherwise sleep again.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project in the kit that isn't tethered to a USB cable. Up until now every sketch has assumed "plugged in, always on." Deep sleep + wake-on-GPIO is the technique behind every battery-powered IoT sensor on the market - door/window sensors, water leak detectors, motion sensors - and the pattern in `setup()` (wake, do one thing, sleep) is the same in every one of them. It's also the first project where the answer to "how do I make this last on a battery?" forced changes to the power topology (drop the boost stage), the wake pin (external pull-down because the internal one sleeps), and the input filtering (RC network because mechanical contacts bounce). Every one of those is a real-world IoT lesson that doesn't come up when the board is plugged into a laptop.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- XIAO ESP32-C3 (3.3 V logic, USB-C powered)
- MPU-6500 IMU breakout (I2C, address 0x68)
- 0.96" SSD1306 OLED, 128x64, I2C (address 0x3C)
- Green LED + 220R current-limiting resistor
- Breadboard and a handful of DuPont jumpers

## Wiring notes

This project is the first time we put two devices on the same I2C bus. I2C is designed for exactly that: every device listens on the same two wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and is told apart by its address. The OLED answers to 0x3C and the MPU-6500 answers to 0x68, so there is no conflict.

- Both the IMU and the OLED get **3.3 V from the XIAO's 3V3 pin**, NOT 5 V. The XIAO's GPIOs are 3.3 V tolerant only; feeding a 5 V I2C device into them can slowly damage the chip.
- Tie all grounds together on the breadboard's blue rail.
- XIAO `SDA` (D4 / GPIO6) goes to BOTH the IMU SDA pin and the OLED SDA pin.
- XIAO `SCL` (D5 / GPIO7) goes to BOTH the IMU SCL pin and the OLED SCL pin.
- The MPU-6500 and OLED breakouts already have pull-up resistors on SDA/SCL on the board, so no extra pull-ups are needed.
- Green LED long leg (anode) to GPIO D2 (GPIO4) through the 220R resistor. Short leg (cathode) to GND.

## Talking points

- **Why two addresses work on one bus:** I2C is like a party line. The XIAO shouts "0x3C, are you there?" and only the OLED answers. Then "0x68, what's your acceleration?" and only the IMU answers. The clock pin keeps everyone in step.
- **Tilt from gravity:** when the board sits flat, gravity pulls straight down through the Z axis of the IMU and X / Y read ~0. Tip the breadboard and some of that 1 g leaks into X or Y. `atan2(ax, az)` and `atan2(ay, az)` give us the tilt angles in radians, which we convert to degrees.
- **Why the bubble goes to the high side:** in a real spirit level the bubble floats to the high end because it is less dense than the liquid. We fake that by drawing the bubble offset in the same direction as the tilt (positive tilt -> bubble offset positive on screen).
- **Why the LED has a deadband:** raw accel data jitters by a fraction of a degree even when still. If we lit the LED at "exactly 0.0 degrees" it would flicker. We light it only when both pitch and roll are within +/-1.0 degrees, and turn it off only above +/-1.5 degrees. That gap is called hysteresis.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a calibration step: average 200 samples at boot and treat that as the new "zero" so the level reads true even if the IMU is glued in slightly crooked.
- Show the numeric angles in the corners of the OLED.
- Add a buzzer that beeps faster as you approach level (audible spirit level for when you can't see the screen).
- Use the gyro as well as the accelerometer (complementary filter) so it stops jiggling when you tap the bench.
- Make it battery-powered with a small LiPo on the XIAO's BAT pad and stick it in a 3D-printed case.

## Why this is interesting

It is a real household tool you can hand to someone and they immediately understand what it does. Under the hood it teaches the three ideas you need for every future IMU project: sharing the I2C bus, turning raw accelerometer numbers into a physical angle, and smoothing noisy data so an output (the LED) doesn't chatter. From here, the same pattern scales up to a self-balancing robot, a step counter, or an orientation-aware game controller.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the "remote" - has the button)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the "lamp" - has the external LED)
- 1x Tactile push-button (wired to the XIAO)
- 1x Red LED (wired to the NodeMCU)
- 1x 220R resistor (current-limit for the LED)
- 1x Breadboard (everything plugs into this, no soldering)
- Jumper wires (M-M for breadboard rails, F-M for board pins)
- Two USB-C cables (one per board)
- Existing GeeFam WiFi network

## Wiring notes

**XIAO side (the button):**
- One leg of the push-button -> XIAO pin `D2` (GPIO 4)
- Other leg of the push-button -> XIAO `GND`
- No external pull-up resistor needed - the sketch turns on the ESP32's internal pull-up (`INPUT_PULLUP`), so a press reads LOW.

**NodeMCU side (the LED):**
- NodeMCU `GPIO 16` -> 220R resistor -> long leg (anode, +) of the LED
- Short leg (cathode, -) of the LED -> NodeMCU `GND`
- The resistor goes in series with the LED. `GPIO -> resistor -> LED -> GND` is the easy mental model.
- Why GPIO16 and not GPIO5? GPIO5 is a "strapping pin" on the classic ESP32 - it's sampled at reset and has an internal pull-up active during boot, which makes any LED on it flicker for a moment every time the board resets. GPIO16 is a plain general-purpose pin with no boot-time role, so it's the cleaner first-project choice.

**Both boards plug into their own USB-C cable.** They never connect to each other physically - they talk over WiFi.

## Bring-up sequence (read before flashing)

This project uses mDNS so we don't have to chase IP addresses. The NodeMCU advertises itself on the LAN as `nodemcu-lamp.local`, and the XIAO talks to that name. No hardcoded peer IP, no chicken-and-egg re-flash cycle.

1. Open the sketch. Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the GeeFam WiFi password (there's a `// TODO` comment marking the spot).
2. **Flash the NodeMCU first:** uncomment `#define ROLE_NODEMCU`, comment out `#define ROLE_XIAO`, upload. Open Serial Monitor (115200) and watch for `mDNS up: http://nodemcu-lamp.local/`. Optional sanity check: from any browser on the same WiFi, open `http://nodemcu-lamp.local/` and you should see the lamp's status text.
3. **Flash the XIAO second:** flip the `ROLE_` defines (XIAO on, NodeMCU off), upload. Open Serial Monitor and you should see it print `Will talk to http://nodemcu-lamp.local/led/toggle`.
4. Press the button on the XIAO. The NodeMCU's LED toggles. The XIAO's serial log shows `-> GET ...` and `peer replied 200 : OK on`.

If mDNS resolution misbehaves on your network, the description for the "Things to change" section below explains how to drop back to hardcoded IPs.

## Talking points

- "Press here, light there." This is the heart of every smart-home gadget: a sensor on one device, an actuator on another, glued together by a network.
- The two boards have different jobs in this build: the XIAO is purely a **client** (it sends one HTTP request when the button is pressed) and the NodeMCU is purely a **server** (it listens for requests and toggles the LED). That asymmetry keeps the sketch small. The "make it bidirectional" version is in "Things to change" below.
- We're using plain HTTP GET requests. When the XIAO sees a button press, it sends `GET /led/toggle` to `nodemcu-lamp.local`. The NodeMCU's web server hears that request, flips the LED, and replies with "OK". No cloud, no app - just two boards on the same WiFi.
- mDNS is why we don't need to type IP addresses. It's a tiny "who is here" announcement system that lets devices on the same LAN find each other by name (`somename.local`). The NodeMCU shouts "I'm `nodemcu-lamp`", the XIAO listens, done.
- This pattern (HTTP requests between devices) scales. Once the Orange Pi is running and hosting a real MQTT broker, you replace the direct HTTP call with "publish to topic" and "subscribe to topic" - same idea, less wiring.

## Things to change once it works

- Make it bidirectional. Right now the XIAO is purely a remote: it has no web server and the NodeMCU never sends it anything. To go two-way, add a `WebServer` on the XIAO with a `/notify` route, and add a second button on the NodeMCU (a free GPIO like 17 or 18, wired the same way as the XIAO's button) that fires an HTTP GET to `xiao-remote.local/notify`. The XIAO has no onboard LED, so use the Serial Monitor as its "output" - or wire a second LED + 220R on a free XIAO pin.
- Replace mDNS with a hardcoded IP if `*.local` resolution is flaky on your network (some routers strip mDNS). Read each board's IP from Serial Monitor at boot, paste the NodeMCU's IP into a `const char* PEER_IP` on the XIAO, and change the URL from `nodemcu-lamp.local` to that IP string.
- Swap "toggle on press" for "pulse for 2 seconds and turn off" so the lamp acts more like a notification than a switch.
- When the Orange Pi is alive, replace the direct board-to-board HTTP with both boards publishing to an MQTT broker on the Pi. This is the actual "hub and leaves" architecture from the kit notes.
- Use the XIAO's deep sleep (wakes on a GPIO change) so a coin cell could power the remote for weeks.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project that uses BOTH ESP32 boards together, which is what the whole kit is structured around. It proves the "leaf endpoint" architecture: each board can independently sense, decide, and talk to peers over WiFi. The mental jump from "one board, one program" to "two boards cooperating" is the same jump you make from a desk calculator to the internet - and once it clicks, every distributed-system idea afterward (MQTT, Home Assistant, REST APIs, microservices) is just a refinement of what you built here.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain, WiFi-capable)
- 1x LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (display)
- 1x DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor (indoor reading - 3-pin breakout preferred)
- 1x 1-channel Relay Module (switches the LED strip)
- 1x LED 5mm Blue (status indicator while talking to the internet)
- 1x 220R resistor (current limit for the blue LED)
- 1x Breadboard 830-point
- DuPont jumper wires (M-M, M-F, F-F mix)
- 1x USB-A to Micro-USB cable (power + programming)

You also need (not in this allocation, supplied separately):
- A short 5V LED strip (or single LED-on-leads). The relay switches its POSITIVE leg between the 5V rail and the strip - see the wiring diagram. Keep it short: about 200 mA max at 5V if you are powering everything from one USB port (see "Power budget" below).
- A free Open-Meteo API endpoint (no key required) - the sketch already points at Andy's home grid square in northern England; change the lat/lon at the top to wherever your hallway is.
- If your DHT11 is the bare 4-pin sensor (not the small breakout PCB), add a 4.7k-10k pull-up resistor from DATA to 3.3V. The blue 3-pin breakout has this on board already.

## Wiring notes

- The LCD's I2C backpack uses only 4 wires: VCC -> 5V, GND -> GND, SDA -> GPIO 21, SCL -> GPIO 22. The ESP32's I2C default is exactly those two pins, no configuration needed.
- The DHT11 needs 3.3V. Some clones tolerate 5V, but 3.3V is safer with an ESP32 because its GPIO is 3.3V; using 5V Vcc with a 3.3V data pin can clamp current through the protection diodes. Data goes to GPIO 4. If you bought the bare 4-pin DHT11 (no PCB), you also need a 4.7k-10k pull-up from DATA to 3.3V; the 3-pin breakout already has one.
- The relay module is low-level trigger (active-LOW). IN -> GPIO 25. We set the pin HIGH *before* `pinMode(..., OUTPUT)` so the relay doesn't click on at boot.
- We are doing **high-side switching of the LED strip's positive leg**: the 5V rail goes into the relay's **COM** terminal, the strip's **+** wire goes to the relay's **NO** (normally open) terminal, and the strip's **-** wire returns directly to GND. When the relay energises, COM connects to NO and the strip lights up. NC is left unused.
- The blue status LED goes from GPIO 2 -> 220R resistor -> LED anode -> LED cathode -> GND. GPIO 2 is also the NodeMCU's built-in blue LED on most clones, so you will see two LEDs blink in sync. That is fine - it confirms your wiring matches the silkscreen.
- **GPIO 2 strapping-pin caveat**: GPIO 2 must be LOW or floating at boot for the chip to flash-boot normally. The 220R-to-LED-to-GND path keeps it pulled low at power-up (the LED's forward voltage drop is below the strap threshold). Do NOT wire a pull-up from GPIO 2 to 3.3V - that will brick boot. Driving it HIGH from `loop()` after boot is fine.
- Common ground! The ESP32 GND, the breadboard GND rail, the relay GND, and the LED strip GND must all be tied together. Floating grounds are the classic "it works once then never again" bug.

## Power budget (read this before adding more LEDs)

A laptop USB-A port supplies roughly 500 mA at 5V. From that the ESP32 itself takes 80-240 mA (bursty on WiFi TX), the LCD backlight 20-40 mA, and the relay coil ~70 mA when energised. That leaves a hard ceiling of around 150-200 mA for the LED strip if you want a stable system - call it 1-2 short WS2812-style segments or a couple of plain 5V LEDs in parallel with their own resistors. If you want a longer strip, switch to a **dedicated 5V/2A supply for the strip**, feed its + into the relay's COM via a separate wire, and **tie its GND to the ESP32 GND** (the relay only switches the + line; the grounds must stay common or nothing turns on).

## Talking points

- The LCD is talked to over **I2C**, a 2-wire serial bus. The same two pins can address up to ~120 devices because each has a unique address (the backpack is usually `0x27` or `0x3F`). The sketch probes both at boot and constructs the LCD object once it knows which address answered.
- The weather data comes from **Open-Meteo**, a free no-key API. We GET an **HTTPS** URL, the server replies with JSON, ArduinoJson plucks out the field we want. HTTPS on ESP32 needs a `WiFiClientSecure`; we call `setInsecure()` on it because we don't care about cert validation for a hobby weather widget.
- **Why a relay for a 5V LED strip?** You don't strictly need one - a transistor would do. But (a) we have a relay in the kit and (b) the satisfying *click* is half the fun for a 10-year-old. It is also the right answer the moment you want to switch a 12V strip or a fan.
- The forecast horizon is the next 12 hours. If the probability of precipitation in any of those hours exceeds 50%, the rain-warning light comes on.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a second display mode (long-press a future button) showing tomorrow's high and low.
- Replace the DHT11 with a DHT22 or BME280 - DHT11 is fine for whole degrees, but the BME280 also gives barometric pressure, which lets you predict weather changes a few hours ahead just from the trend.
- Swap the polling loop for a deep-sleep-then-publish-then-sleep cycle if you ever want to run this on battery.
- Send the indoor readings to Mosquitto on the Orange Pi One once that hub is online (see the kit-level CLAUDE.md - the Pi is the intended hub).
- Add a buzzer that beeps once when the relay first switches on, then stays quiet.
- Pin the Open-Meteo root CA instead of using `setInsecure()`, so a tampered DNS reply cannot feed you a bogus forecast.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project in the kit that **leaves the room**. Up to here, everything has been a closed loop: a button presses, an LED lights, a sensor reads, a relay clicks. Here, the ESP32 reaches out across the internet over TLS, asks a public weather service a question, parses the answer, and acts on it - all in about 250 lines of C++. Combining that internet data with a local sensor reading (the DHT11) is the entire essence of IoT in one project. After this, the rest of the kit's projects become variations on the same theme.

projects.name: MQTT Home: Pi broker + XIAO sensor publisher
projects.power_supply: Orange Pi One: 5V / 2A wall adapter via the 4.0/1.7mm barrel jack (NOT micro-USB). XIAO ESP32-C3: 5V over USB-C from a laptop or phone charger. DHT11 draws power from the XIAO's 3V3 rail. Router + WiFi assumed already powered.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- Orange Pi One (H3) - the protagonist. Already booted into Armbian with `mosquitto` and `mosquitto-clients` installed (see the resume checklist in the OrangePi_One folder).
- Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 - the leaf sensor node.
- DHT11 temperature + humidity sensor (3-pin module variant has its own pull-up; bare 4-pin DHT11 needs a 10K resistor between DATA and 3V3).
- 1x 10K resistor (1/8W) for the DHT11 pull-up.
- Mini breadboard + a handful of M-M jumpers to hold the XIAO and DHT11.
- Router / WiFi on `GeeFam` (2.4 GHz) - Pi on Ethernet, XIAO on WiFi, both on the same subnet.

## Wiring notes

This project is mostly a network wiring diagram, not a breadboard one. Three things have to be true:

1. **Pi on the LAN.** Plug the Pi's Ethernet into the same router that broadcasts `GeeFam`. Power it from the 5V/2A barrel supply (NOT micro-USB - see the OrangePi_One CLAUDE notes about silent brownouts). Find its IP on the router admin page the same way you found the XIAO at `192.168.88.30`.
2. **Mosquitto listening on the Pi.** After SSH-ing in with `ssh root@<pi-ip>`, run:
   ```bash
   apt update && apt install -y mosquitto mosquitto-clients
   # Allow LAN clients (for learning only - no auth yet):
   cat > /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/lan.conf <<'EOF'
   listener 1883 0.0.0.0
   allow_anonymous true
   EOF
   systemctl restart mosquitto
   systemctl enable  mosquitto
   ```
   Confirm with `ss -tlnp | grep 1883`. You should see mosquitto bound to `0.0.0.0:1883`.
3. **DHT11 on the XIAO.**
   - `DHT11 VCC -> XIAO 3V3`
   - `DHT11 GND -> XIAO GND`
   - `DHT11 DATA -> XIAO D1 (GPIO 3)`
   - 10K resistor between `DATA` and `3V3` (skip if your DHT11 is the 3-pin pre-pulled-up variant)

Update `MQTT_HOST` in the sketch to the Pi's IP before flashing. Open Serial Monitor at 115200, then on the Pi run:

```bash
mosquitto_sub -h localhost -t 'home/livingroom/#' -v
```

You should see `home/livingroom/status online` immediately, followed by temperature + humidity every 30 seconds.

## Talking points

- **Pub/sub vs request/response.** The XIAO doesn't know or care who's listening. It pushes readings to a topic; anything that cares (a dashboard, Home Assistant, a Node-RED flow on the same Pi) subscribes. Adding a second display device later is zero changes to the publisher.
- **Last-will testament.** `connect()` registers `home/livingroom/status = "offline"` as a "send this if I die". If the XIAO loses power or WiFi, the broker fires that message after the keepalive expires. That's how the Pi can know the node is gone without polling it.
- **Retained messages.** Both readings are published with the retained flag. A subscriber that connects ten minutes later still gets the last known value immediately instead of waiting up to 30 seconds for the next one.
- **The hub/leaf split is now real.** Up until now every project on the kit ran end-to-end on a single board. This one stops working unless both halves are alive on the network at the same time. That's the architectural shift that makes the rest of the kit's planned services (Home Assistant, Grafana) possible.

## Things to change once it works

- **Add a second leaf.** Flash a similar sketch onto the NodeMCU-32S with topic `home/garage/temperature` and watch both streams in one `mosquitto_sub -t 'home/#' -v` window.
- **Turn on auth.** Replace `allow_anonymous true` with a password file (`mosquitto_passwd -c /etc/mosquitto/passwd andy`), and pass the credentials into `mqtt.connect()`.
- **Persist to disk.** `apt install sqlite3`, then run a tiny Python loop on the Pi that subscribes and inserts rows into a SQLite table. That's the foundation of the future InfluxDB + Grafana setup without committing to the heavy stack yet.
- **Add the OLED.** Wire the 0.96" OLED to the NodeMCU-32S and have it subscribe to `home/livingroom/temperature` so it shows the XIAO's reading on its own screen. First "device A talks to device B via the Pi" moment.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project on the kit where the Orange Pi earns its place. Up to now it's been a powered-off board with a barrel-jack gotcha. After this, it's the always-on hub that every other ESP32 project can publish into, and every dashboard you ever add to the kit subscribes from. The DHT11 is intentionally boring - the point isn't the sensor, it's that the wiring diagram from now on is a network diagram, not a breadboard one.

projects.name: Joystick Doodle Pad on OLED
projects.power_supply: ESP32 is powered from a laptop via USB; the joystick module and OLED both run off the ESP32's 3.3V rail through the breadboard.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Joystick Module (2-axis + button) - the star: two potentiometers (X and Y) and a push-button under the cap
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the joystick and drives the screen
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - the 128x64 canvas you paint on
- 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - share 3.3V and GND between three things cleanly
- 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - power rails on the breadboard
- 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc - female ends plug into the joystick/OLED header pins

## Wiring notes

Everything in this build runs off the ESP32's 3.3V rail. Most generic 0.96" SSD1306 OLED modules accept 3.3-5V on VCC because they have an onboard regulator, but we are using 3.3V everywhere so the whole project shares one rail - cleaner and one less thing to think about.

A note on the joystick's VCC pin: most of these modules are silkscreened "+5V". Ignore that label and wire it to 3.3V anyway. The joystick is just two potentiometers and a push-button, so it doesn't care what voltage you feed it - the ADC reading is a ratio of the supply voltage, and the code reads it the same way at 3.3V as it would at 5V. If you DO connect the joystick's VCC to 5V on an ESP32, the button's SW pin will sit near 5V when the button is pressed, and that 5V will land on GPIO 32 - a 3.3V-only input. That's the kind of mistake that quietly stresses the chip, so just stick to 3.3V.

Joystick to ESP32:

- `+5V` (yes, even though it says +5V on the silkscreen) -> 3.3V rail
- `GND` -> GND rail
- `VRX` -> GPIO 34 (X axis, an input-only ADC pin - perfect for this)
- `VRY` -> GPIO 35 (Y axis, input-only ADC pin)
- `SW`  -> GPIO 32 (the click-down button under the stick)

OLED to ESP32:

- `VCC` -> 3.3V rail
- `GND` -> GND rail
- `SDA` -> GPIO 21 (default ESP32 I2C data line)
- `SCL` -> GPIO 22 (default ESP32 I2C clock line)

The joystick button has no external pull-up resistor, so the code turns on the ESP32's internal pull-up (`INPUT_PULLUP`). That means "released" reads HIGH and "pressed" reads LOW - watch for that in the talking points.

## Talking points

- Move the stick: a blinking dot (the cursor) moves around the screen.
- Click the button: the pen toggles between "up" and "down". With the pen down, the cursor leaves a trail of white pixels - that's the drawing.
- Hold the button for one second: the screen wipes clean and the pen lifts. Good for "oops, start over".
- The cursor blinks so you can see where you are even on a blank canvas.
- The deadzone in the code (`DEADZONE = 250`) means the cursor only moves when you push the stick noticeably. Without it, ADC noise alone would make the cursor drift.
- How the drawing survives the blinking cursor: the code keeps its own `canvas[128][64]` array of which pixels have been "painted". Every frame it wipes the OLED, redraws the whole canvas from that array, then stamps the cursor on top. The cursor is never stored in the canvas, so it can never leave phantom dots.

## Things to change once it works

- Make the pen "thicker": draw a 2x2 or 3x3 block of canvas cells instead of a single one when the pen is down.
- Diagonal-only mode for a 10-year-old's first maze drawing - only commit pixels when X or Y exceeds a threshold.
- Add a small status line in the top corner showing PEN UP / PEN DOWN (just draw text after the canvas copy, before the cursor).
- Speed-sensitive cursor: square the stick deflection so tiny pushes nudge gently and full deflection zooms.
- Save the drawing to LittleFS so it survives a reboot, then add a "gallery" mode that cycles through saved drawings.
- Two-player Etch-A-Sketch: one joystick controls X, a second joystick controls Y, and you have to cooperate.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first project that asks the ESP32 to read TWO analog inputs at once and translate that into something visually obvious. The joystick teaches three ideas that show up everywhere later: an analog reading is a number from 0 to 4095, a "center" reading is rarely exactly half (so you need a deadzone), and a button without an external resistor needs the chip's internal pull-up to behave. Combining that with the OLED gives instant, satisfying feedback - the kind where a 10-year-old can sit down and start drawing within 10 seconds of plugging it in.

projects.name: Laser Tripwire Alarm
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the Arduino Uno; the Uno's 5V rail powers the laser, photoresistor, and alarm LED.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- Arduino Uno R3 (the brain, 5V GPIO)
- KY-008 Red Laser Module (the beam - the star of the show)
- KY-018 Photoresistor Module (the beam catcher)
- 5mm red LED + 330R resistor (the alarm indicator)
- Breadboard, jumper wires

## Wiring notes

- **Laser (KY-008)**: three pins, labeled S (signal), middle (often unused or +), and `-` (GND). On most KY-008 boards the laser turns on whenever **S is HIGH and `-` is GND**. Wire S to Arduino pin 7 and `-` to Arduino GND. The middle pin is usually not connected, leave it floating.
- **Photoresistor (KY-018)**: three pins - `S` (analog out), middle = VCC (5V), `-` = GND. Wire S to A0, middle to 5V, `-` to GND.
- **Alarm LED**: long leg (anode) to Arduino pin 9 through the 330R resistor on the breadboard. Short leg (cathode) to GND. The resistor is non-negotiable - bare LEDs on a GPIO pin die fast.
- **Aim**: with everything wired up, hold the laser so the red dot lands exactly on the small black sensor on top of the KY-018 module. The closer the dot is to the sensor, the bigger the difference between "beam on" and "beam broken" - which makes the tripwire more sensitive.

## Talking points

- "Why does the laser need GND?" Every circuit needs a complete loop. Electricity leaves the 5V/signal pin, does its work in the laser, and has to come back home through GND. Without GND, no loop, no light.
- "Why doesn't the laser go through my hand?" Red 650nm laser light is visible, fairly low energy, and very directional. Your skin absorbs and scatters it, so almost none reaches the sensor on the other side - that's exactly why this works as a tripwire.
- "Why calibrate at startup?" Different rooms have different ambient light. The sketch reads the photoresistor 20 times in the first second, averages those, and uses that as the "beam is hitting the target" baseline. Then any big drop from that baseline means something interrupted the beam.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer or relay-driven siren in parallel with the alarm LED so it makes noise.
- Replace `delay(50)` with a latch: once tripped, stay tripped until a button is pressed to re-arm.
- Aim the laser at a mirror placed across the room and bounce the beam back into the photoresistor - turn a doorway into a long tripwire.
- Log the time of each break to Serial and graph it later.

## Why this is interesting

This is the project that makes a 10-year-old say "this is the coolest thing I've ever built." A real red laser, a real invisible tripwire across the kitchen, an alarm that goes off when someone walks through. It teaches three big ideas at once - digital output (turning the laser on), analog input (reading varying light levels), and calibration (the code adapts to whatever room you're in instead of using magic numbers).

## Eye-safety note

The KY-008 is a low-power Class 2 (or similar) red laser, but **never aim it at anyone's eyes**, including pets. Aim it across a flat surface like a tabletop where the only thing that can break it is a hand or a toy car driving through.

<![CDATA[// Laser Tripwire Alarm
// Aim the KY-008 red laser at the KY-018 photoresistor.
// When something blocks the beam, the red alarm LED turns on
// and the Serial Monitor prints "BEAM BROKEN!".
//
// Board: Arduino Uno R3 (5V logic)
// Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud to see readings.

const int PIN_LASER     = 7;   // KY-008 signal pin (S)
const int PIN_LDR       = A0;  // KY-018 analog out
const int PIN_ALARM_LED = 9;   // 5mm red LED through 330R to GND

// Tuning: higher number on A0 = MORE light hitting the photoresistor.
// We calibrate at startup, then trip if the reading falls well below
// the bright baseline.
int brightBaseline = 0;
const int TRIP_MARGIN = 150;   // how far below baseline counts as "blocked"

void setup() {
  pinMode(PIN_LASER, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(PIN_ALARM_LED, OUTPUT);

  Serial.begin(9600);
  delay(500);
  Serial.println(F("Laser Tripwire starting..."));

  // Turn the laser on and let the photoresistor settle.
  digitalWrite(PIN_LASER, HIGH);
  delay(800);

  // Take a few readings of the "beam clear" state and average them.
  long sum = 0;
  const int samples = 20;
  for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    sum += analogRead(PIN_LDR);
    delay(25);
  }
  brightBaseline = sum / samples;

  Serial.print(F("Bright baseline (beam on target) = "));
  Serial.println(brightBaseline);
  Serial.print(F("Will trip if reading drops below "));
  Serial.println(brightBaseline - TRIP_MARGIN);
  Serial.println(F("Aim the laser at the photoresistor and wave your hand through the beam."));
}

void loop() {
  int reading = analogRead(PIN_LDR);
  bool broken = (reading < brightBaseline - TRIP_MARGIN);

  if (broken) {
    digitalWrite(PIN_ALARM_LED, HIGH);
    Serial.print(F("BEAM BROKEN!  reading="));
    Serial.println(reading);
  } else {
    digitalWrite(PIN_ALARM_LED, LOW);
  }

  delay(50);
}
]]>

projects.name: Reaction-Time Game v2 (Proto PCB Edition)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the Arduino Uno's USB-B socket - the Uno regulates and feeds the proto PCB's 5V/GND rails.
projects.description:
**Soldering project - up front warning.** This is the one project in the kit that uses a soldering iron. Everything else has been solderless (breadboard + DuPont jumpers). The point of this build is to take a circuit Andy already knows works - the reaction-time game that was his first build - and make it *permanent* on a double-sided proto PCB so it lives on a shelf instead of occupying the breadboard. Treat it as Andy's intermediate solo project. His son can watch and read out reaction times, but the iron stays in adult hands.

The Arduino itself is **not** soldered. We solder female header sockets onto the proto PCB and the Uno plugs into them, so the brain is reusable for the next thing. Only the buttons, LEDs, resistors, and short wire links get soldered.

Workflow (this is half the lesson):

1. Rebuild the game on a breadboard one last time using these exact pins. Confirm green/red/buttons all behave.
2. Plan the layout on the PCB *before* heating the iron - a sharpie dot on each hole that gets a part.
3. Solder the lowest-profile parts first (resistors), then headers and buttons, LEDs last.
4. Flip the board, route point-to-point with the stripped insides of an M-M jumper wire. Keep wires short.
5. Inspect every joint under a lamp - should be shiny and concave, not a dull blob. Re-flow anything that looks like a "cold" joint.
6. Plug the Uno in *last*. Power up. If anything draws weird current, unplug fast.

## Parts list

- 1x Double-Sided Prototype PCB (the star - the new home of the circuit)
- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (sits in a socket on the PCB, not soldered in)
- 2x Tactile push-button (START + PLAYER)
- 1x Green 5mm LED (GO light)
- 1x Red 5mm LED (WAIT / FAIL light)
- 2x 330R resistor (LED current limit)
- 2x 10K resistor (button pull-ups - belt-and-braces alongside `INPUT_PULLUP`)
- 1x Female header strip, cut into two short rails to socket the Uno's D-pins
- 1x Male header strip, cut for the PCB I/O block
- Hookup wire (stripped from an M-M jumper) for point-to-point links on the underside
- 1x Breadboard for the pre-solder dry run

## Wiring notes

- Both buttons are wired **active-LOW**: one leg goes to its Uno pin, the other to GND. The Uno's internal pull-up (`INPUT_PULLUP`) plus the external 10K resistor to the **5V rail** pulls the pin HIGH when the button is open. Pressing the button shorts it to GND.
- LEDs face the same way every time: long leg (anode) toward the Uno pin via the 330R, short leg (cathode) to GND.
- Keep the LED resistor right next to its LED on the PCB - that way if the resistor ever fries you can find it instantly.
- The Uno's 5V and GND rails get a single soldered tie-point on the PCB, and everything else fans out from there. No daisy-chained ground hops.
- Flux helps. Lead-free solder sticks better with extra flux dabbed on the pad.

## Talking points

- "Why are we soldering this one?" Because a breadboard contact relies on a spring. Springs lose tension, and a circuit you want to keep deserves a real metal joint.
- A *cold solder joint* looks like crumbly grey play-dough. A *good* joint looks shiny and pulled toward the pad - like a tiny silver volcano. Re-heat anything that looks crumbly.
- The Arduino plugs into a socket, not directly into the board. That socket is the most expensive bit of foresight in the whole build - it means we can pull the Uno back out for the next project.
- `INPUT_PULLUP` does the same job as the external 10K in software. We use both. On a breadboard, software alone is fine. On a permanent board that might sit near a noisy power supply, the physical resistor adds confidence.
- The first sketch already debounced the buttons in code. On the soldered board that matters more, because a flaky button starts to look like a "ghost press".
- Note on the debounce helper: the v2 sketch keys its per-button state by a small index (0 and 1) passed in by the caller, not by the raw GPIO pin number. That means swapping a button to a different Uno pin only changes one constant at the top of the file - the debounce arrays don't have to be re-sized or re-thought.

## Things to change once it works

- Add the 4-digit 7-segment display module from the kit to show reaction time in milliseconds instead of using the Serial Monitor.
- Add a third button for "two-player mode" - first one to hit GO wins.
- Drill two small holes in a project box and mount the PCB inside, LEDs and buttons poking through the lid.
- Power it from a 9V battery via the Uno's barrel jack so it doesn't need a laptop.
- Log the last 10 reaction times in EEPROM so the leaderboard survives a power cycle.

## Why this is interesting

The leap from "it works on a breadboard" to "it works on a board I keep in a drawer" is the leap from hobbyist tinkering to actually owning a thing you built. Soldering is the rite-of-passage skill that makes that leap possible, and a proto PCB is the friendliest place to learn it - the holes are pre-drilled, the pads are pre-tinned, and the spacing matches every through-hole part you own. Doing it on a circuit Andy already understands means the only new variable is the *technique*, not the *design*. If the soldered version misbehaves, he knows the bug is in the joints or the wiring, not in the code or the parts list. That's a very calm way to learn a slightly intimidating skill.

projects.name: Clap-O-Meter (Live Sound Bar Graph)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard 3.3V regulator powers the KY-037 mic, the OLED, and the red LED through a 330R resistor.
projects.description:
A live loudness meter built around the KY-037 microphone. The ESP32 reads the mic, scales the result onto a bar across the OLED, and flashes a red LED whenever the sound crosses a "loud" threshold - so a clap, a shout or a slammed door becomes a thing you can see.

## Parts list

- KY-037 Microphone Sensor (the protagonist) - analog audio input
- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the mic, drives the OLED, controls the LED
- 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - the bar graph and the labels
- 5mm red LED + 330R resistor - flashes on loud sound
- 10uF electrolytic capacitor - decoupling across the mic VCC/GND for a cleaner signal
- Breadboard, a pack of M-M jumpers, a pack of F-M jumpers

## Wiring notes

- The KY-037 runs happily off the ESP32's 3.3V rail. Put VCC and GND on the breadboard power rails first.
- Drop the 10uF electrolytic cap straight across the mic's VCC and GND pins on the breadboard. Longer leg goes to VCC, shorter leg to GND. This soaks up the little voltage wobbles the mic causes when WiFi or the OLED is busy, and the analog reading visibly settles down.
- The mic's A0 (analog out) goes to GPIO34. That pin is input-only on the ESP32, which is exactly what you want for a sensor - nothing in your sketch can accidentally drive it.
- The OLED is I2C: SDA -> GPIO21, SCL -> GPIO22. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins.
- The red LED gets the usual treatment: GPIO23 -> 330R resistor -> long leg of LED -> short leg to GND. Without the resistor the LED burns out and possibly the GPIO with it.
- Leave the D0 pin on the KY-037 unconnected. That's the built-in comparator with the blue trimpot, and we don't use it - the sketch does the threshold work in software so you can tweak it without a screwdriver.

## Talking points

- The mic doesn't output "loudness" - it outputs the audio waveform, swinging above and below a quiet midpoint many hundreds of times a second. We sample on a steady 1 ms tick (~1000 Hz) and measure how far each sample is from the calibrated quiet baseline. That absolute swing is what we draw.
- The bar uses a "peak with decay" trick: every new high pushes the bar up instantly, but a steady countdown drags it back down 20 ms at a time. That's why a clap shoots the bar up and then it slides back - matches how our ears feel loudness.
- The calibration at boot is just a 1-second average of the quiet room. Cover the mic or shout at it during boot and the baseline will be wrong - reset and let the room be quiet for a second.

## Things to change once it works

- Lower `LOUD_THRESHOLD` until a finger snap sets the LED off, or raise it so only a real clap counts.
- Add a second LED at a higher threshold for "very loud" so you have a two-stage indicator.
- Count claps in a 1-second window and use a double-clap as a "switch" - feed that into a relay to make a clap-on-clap-off lamp.
- Log the peak loudness once a second over WiFi to a tiny web page and watch the room's noise level over an evening.

## Why this is interesting

It turns something invisible (sound) into something visible and instantly playable. A 10-year-old can clap and see the bar move - no explanation needed. Underneath it's the same picture a real audio meter on a mixing desk is drawing, which makes it a great springboard into "how does a microphone actually work" without any math.

projects.name: Laser Posture Coach (desk slouch detector)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered via its USB-C port from a laptop or 5 V phone charger; the VL53L0X, OLED, LEDs and button are fed from the ESP32's 3.3 V rail.
projects.description:
A laser-based desk posture coach. The VL53L0X sits flat on the desk pointing straight up. When you sit upright, it sees your chest at (say) 500 mm. When you slouch forward toward the screen, that distance shrinks. A green LED + "GOOD" message means upright; a red LED + "SLOUCH!" warning means you've crept too close. A button lets you recalibrate the "upright" distance for your chair height.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (brain, drives I2C and LEDs)
- VL53L0X ToF distance sensor (GY-VL53L0XV2 module) - the protagonist
- 0.96" I2C OLED display - shows live distance and posture verdict
- 1x green 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (good-posture light)
- 1x red 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (slouch warning)
- 1x tactile push-button (3x6x4.3 mm) - recalibrate
- Breadboard + DuPont jumper wires

## Wiring notes

- The ESP32 is powered from a laptop USB port via the on-board USB-C jack. Everything else is fed from the ESP32's 3.3 V and GND rails.
- Both the OLED and the VL53L0X are I2C devices. They share SDA (GPIO 21) and SCL (GPIO 22). They have different I2C addresses (OLED 0x3C, VL53L0X 0x29), so they coexist on the same two wires without any extra hardware.
- The VL53L0X module already has on-board pull-up resistors on SDA/SCL and a 3.3 V regulator + level shifters, so it's safe to power from either 3.3 V or 5 V. We use 3.3 V because the ESP32 is a 3.3 V device.
- LEDs: long leg (anode) to the GPIO through a 330R resistor; short leg (cathode) to GND. Green on GPIO 25, red on GPIO 26.
- Button between GPIO 27 and GND. We turn on the ESP32's internal pull-up so we don't need an external one. Pressed = LOW.
- Aim the sensor straight up. Sit at your normal typing position, press the button to set the target distance, then try slouching forward - the red LED should light when your chest gets ~8 cm closer than the target.

## Talking points

- "Time of Flight" really does mean what it says: this chip fires a tiny invisible 940 nm laser pulse and measures how long the photons take to bounce back. Light moves about 30 cm in 1 nanosecond - the chip times that.
- Unlike the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (which uses sound and gives ~1 cm resolution), the VL53L0X reports in millimeters and works fine at close range. That precision is what makes "you slouched 8 cm" detectable instead of "you moved, maybe."
- Two different chips, one pair of wires. I2C lets multiple devices share SDA and SCL by giving each a unique address. The OLED answers at 0x3C; the ToF answers at 0x29.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer (a piezo against a GPIO) that beeps after you've been slouching for more than 10 seconds.
- Log slouch events to the serial monitor with timestamps, then graph "minutes slouched per hour."
- Push posture stats to the Orange Pi (when it's booted) over WiFi/MQTT and build a daily report.
- Use the second VL53L0X (we have two) mounted sideways to also detect when you lean too far back.

## Why this is interesting

This sensor is the cheapest way an Andy-budget project can do real laser ranging - the same family of chips lives in robot vacuums and phone autofocus systems. Pairing it with an OLED on the same I2C bus is a clean first lesson in "multiple devices share two wires," which is the foundation for almost every more advanced sensor project that follows.

projects.name: Magnet Swipe Counter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V USB charger into the ESP32's USB port; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the KY-003 and the OLED.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x KY-003 Hall Switch Sensor (the protagonist - a tiny chip that snaps LOW when the south pole of a magnet gets close)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor and drives the screen)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (shows the live count)
- 1x Green 5mm LED + 1x 330R resistor (flashes once per swipe for instant tactile feedback)
- 1x breadboard
- A handful of jumper wires
- Any small magnet from around the house (fridge magnet, motor magnet, the round neodymium ones from old hard drives)

## Wiring notes

The KY-003 module has 3 pins - usually labelled S (signal), middle (VCC) and minus (GND). The middle pin is power, even though it looks like the obvious "data" pin. Double-check the silkscreen before plugging in.

- KY-003 `-` to ESP32 `GND`
- KY-003 middle (`+` or `VCC`) to ESP32 `3V3`
- KY-003 `S` to ESP32 `GPIO 14`

The OLED uses the ESP32's default I2C pins:

- OLED `VCC` to ESP32 `3V3`
- OLED `GND` to ESP32 `GND`
- OLED `SDA` to ESP32 `GPIO 21`
- OLED `SCL` to ESP32 `GPIO 22`

The LED sits on the breadboard:

- ESP32 `GPIO 27` to the long leg (anode) of the green LED
- Short leg (cathode) through the 330R resistor to `GND`

The KY-003 has its own pull-up resistor on board, so you don't need an external one. The sketch also enables the ESP32's internal pull-up as a safety net.

## Talking points

- Hall sensors are how your laptop knows the lid is closed and how your phone knows when the magnetic case is shut. They are everywhere and never wear out because nothing physically touches anything.
- The KY-003 only reacts to one pole of the magnet (the south pole). If your magnet doesn't seem to trigger it, flip the magnet over - that is almost always the fix.
- "Active LOW" means the signal pin is normally HIGH (3.3V) and drops to LOW (0V) when the sensor sees a magnet. This is backwards from how most people think about switches, so it's a great example of "the world doesn't always agree with you".
- The 40 ms debounce window in the code is there because a magnet swept past quickly can make the digital line jitter for a millisecond or two. Without debouncing, one swipe could count as three.

## Things to change once it works

- Try different magnets - a small ceramic fridge magnet vs. a tiny neodymium - and see how close you have to get for each. That distance is the sensor's effective range.
- Change `PIN_HALL` to a different pin (e.g. `4` or `15`) and update the wiring to match. Get into the habit of changing both at once.
- Add a "high score" reset by holding the magnet near the sensor for 3 seconds: detect a long LOW instead of a short pulse and zero the counter.
- Replace the OLED with the LCD 1602 + I2C backpack and rewrite `drawScreen()` for the LCD - same data, different display.
- Log each swipe out over WiFi (MQTT to the Orange Pi once it boots) so you have a "door opened" history.

## Why this is interesting

Magnetic sensing is the cleanest "yes / no" the universe gives you in beginner electronics. There is no light to interfere with it, no sound to confuse it, no contact to wear out. Pair that with the OLED and you get a project where every action causes an immediate, satisfying visual change - which is the single most motivating thing when you are learning. It also sets up two real-world projects you will eventually want: a door/window open sensor, and a wheel-rotation speedometer.

<![CDATA[// Magnet Swipe Counter
// Wave a magnet past the KY-003 Hall switch. Each swipe increments a counter
// shown on the OLED, and the green LED flashes once per swipe.
//
// Board: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
// Libraries (install via Library Manager):
//   - Adafruit GFX Library
//   - Adafruit SSD1306

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>

// ---------- Pin assignments (match the wiring diagram) ----------
const int PIN_HALL = 14;  // KY-003 signal output (active LOW when magnet present)
const int PIN_LED  = 27;  // Green LED via 330R to GND

// ---------- OLED setup ----------
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET   -1
#define OLED_ADDR    0x3C
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// ---------- State ----------
unsigned long swipeCount = 0;
int lastHallState = HIGH;          // KY-003 idles HIGH (no magnet)
unsigned long lastEdgeMs = 0;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 40;
unsigned long ledOffAtMs = 0;
const unsigned long LED_FLASH_MS = 120;

void drawScreen(bool magnetNow) {
    display.clearDisplay();

    // Header
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
    display.setCursor(0, 0);
    display.print("Magnet Swipe Counter");
    display.drawLine(0, 10, 127, 10, SSD1306_WHITE);

    // Big count
    display.setTextSize(3);
    display.setCursor(0, 18);
    display.print(swipeCount);

    // Status icon
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setCursor(0, 54);
    if (magnetNow) {
        display.print("[ MAGNET DETECTED ]");
    } else {
        display.print("Wave a magnet by...");
    }

    display.display();
}

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(115200);

    pinMode(PIN_HALL, INPUT_PULLUP); // KY-003 has its own pull-up, but belt-and-braces
    pinMode(PIN_LED, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);

    Wire.begin();  // SDA=21, SCL=22 on ESP32 by default

    if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDR)) {
        Serial.println("OLED not found. Check wiring (SDA=21, SCL=22).");
        while (true) {
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            delay(200);
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
            delay(200);
        }
    }

    drawScreen(false);
    Serial.println("Ready. Wave a magnet near the KY-003.");
}

void loop() {
    int hallState = digitalRead(PIN_HALL);
    unsigned long now = millis();

    // Detect a falling edge (HIGH -> LOW = magnet just arrived) with debounce
    if (hallState != lastHallState && (now - lastEdgeMs) > DEBOUNCE_MS) {
        lastEdgeMs = now;
        if (hallState == LOW) {
            swipeCount++;
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            ledOffAtMs = now + LED_FLASH_MS;
            Serial.print("Swipe #");
            Serial.println(swipeCount);
            drawScreen(true);
        } else {
            drawScreen(false);
        }
        lastHallState = hallState;
    }

    // Turn the LED off after its flash window
    if (ledOffAtMs != 0 && now >= ledOffAtMs) {
        digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
        ledOffAtMs = 0;
    }
}

projects.power_supply: USB cable from Andy's PC to the Arduino Uno - the Uno's onboard 5V rail powers the KY-022 and all four LEDs.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x KY-022 IR Receiver Module (the star - a tiny 38 kHz IR demodulator on a breakout board)
- 1x Arduino Uno R3 (5V GPIO; the `IRremote` library is rock-solid on AVR)
- 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points)
- 1x F-M jumper pack (for the 3-pin KY-022 header)
- 1x M-M jumper pack (for the LEDs and resistors on the breadboard)
- 1x Red, 1x Green, 1x Blue, 1x Yellow 5mm LED
- 4x 330R resistors (one per LED)

## Wiring notes

The KY-022 has three pins. Different clone boards label them slightly differently, but the order is always the same: **S** (signal), middle pin is **VCC** on most boards, and the one marked with a `-` is **GND**. If yours has the `-` on the outside instead of the signal, just look at the silkscreen - it's always labelled.

- KY-022 **S** -> Arduino **D2** (the `IRremote` library can use almost any pin; D2 is conventional)
- KY-022 **VCC** -> Arduino **5V**
- KY-022 **GND** -> Arduino **GND**

Each LED gets its own resistor between the Arduino pin and the LED's long leg (anode). The short leg (cathode) goes to the breadboard's GND rail.

- D6 -> 330R -> Red LED anode; Red cathode -> GND rail
- D7 -> 330R -> Green LED anode; Green cathode -> GND rail
- D8 -> 330R -> Blue LED anode; Blue cathode -> GND rail
- D9 -> 330R -> Yellow LED anode; Yellow cathode -> GND rail
- Arduino GND -> breadboard GND rail

When the sketch boots it briefly flashes all four LEDs in sequence as a wiring self-test. If one stays dark, that's the row to recheck before worrying about the IR side.

## Talking points

- **Why the dome is dark plastic.** That bubble on the KY-022 is a filter that lets infrared through and blocks visible light. Without it, sunlight or a desk lamp would drown out the remote.
- **Why 38 kHz matters.** Remotes don't send a steady "on" - they send the signal as a 38,000-times-a-second flicker. The receiver is tuned to that flicker, so steady light sources don't fool it.
- **Pressing the same button gives the same code.** That's the whole point of a remote protocol. The sketch learns four of those codes and reacts when it sees them again.
- **Pin 13 blinks for free.** The `ENABLE_LED_FEEDBACK` flag makes the Uno's built-in LED blink every time *any* IR frame arrives. Even an unknown button proves the receiver is alive.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a fifth "off" button that turns every LED off, by extending the learn sequence to five buttons.
- Swap the LEDs for the 2-channel Songle relay (low-voltage DC only - the bedside lamp stays on its own switch) and turn this into a remote-controlled fan or LED strip switch.
- Print the raw `0x...` codes for *every* button on your remote on the Serial Monitor and make a little reference table. You'll see the same prefix on every button - that's the remote's "address".
- Wire up the LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack and have it show the name of the last colour pressed instead of just lighting an LED.

## Why this is interesting

Most beginner sensor projects work in *one* direction: the world changes, the sensor responds. IR receivers flip that around - they give you a way to *send commands in* to the Arduino from across the room, using equipment (a TV remote) that's already in the house. Once you can decode a remote, an enormous chunk of consumer electronics suddenly stops being a black box. And because you're capturing real codes off a real remote, every household ends up with a slightly different demo, which keeps it fresh when Andy's son wants to show it off.

projects.name: Invisible Tripwire Alarm with OLED Face
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard regulator feeds the IR module, OLED, and LED from its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
A doorway "invisible tripwire" that watches a small patch of air in front of the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module. The moment your hand (or your son's hand) crosses the beam, the OLED face flips from calm "ARMED" to shocked "INTRUDER!", a red LED lights up, and a trip counter on the screen ticks up. Pull your hand away and everything snaps back. It's the same satisfying "did I really do that?" feedback as a museum motion sensor, built in an afternoon.

## Parts list

- 1x IR Obstacle Avoidance Module (the protagonist - a digital "is something in front of me?" sensor)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED)
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (for the ARMED / INTRUDER faces and trip counter)
- 1x 5mm red LED (lights while the beam is broken)
- 1x 330R resistor (current-limit for the red LED)
- 1x breadboard, plus F-M and M-M jumper wires

## Wiring notes

- The IR module has a 3-pin header: `VCC`, `GND`, `OUT`. Power it from the ESP32's `3V3` pin and `GND`. (The module accepts 3.3V-5V; 3.3V keeps logic levels safe for the ESP32.)
- `OUT` goes to `GPIO 32`. The module has its own pull-up, so use `INPUT` (no internal pull-up needed).
- The OLED is I2C: `SDA` -> `GPIO 21`, `SCL` -> `GPIO 22`, plus `3V3` and `GND`. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins, so `Wire.begin()` without arguments is enough.
- Red LED: `GPIO 25` -> 330R -> LED anode (long leg) -> LED cathode (short leg) -> `GND`. Resistor first protects the LED if the wire slips.
- The IR module has a small blue trimpot on the back. Turn it with a tiny screwdriver to adjust trigger distance from a couple of centimetres up to about 30 cm. There are also two indicator LEDs on the module itself: a power LED and an "obstacle detected" LED. The obstacle LED lighting up is a great sanity check before you even look at the OLED.

## Talking points

- *Active-LOW logic, again.* Just like the 2-ch relay board: the sensor's `OUT` line sits HIGH normally and pulls LOW when something is detected. Show your son `digitalRead(PIN_IR_OUT) == LOW` and ask him "so... does LOW mean nothing's there, or something IS there?" It's the classic beginner trap that's easier to learn once than to memorise forever.
- *Why debounce?* The IR detector edge isn't perfectly clean - as a hand enters or leaves the beam you might get a few rapid HIGH/LOW flickers across a millisecond or two. Without the 40ms debounce window, one wave of the hand could log 5 trips. With it, you log exactly 1.
- *Why a small built-in face on the OLED instead of just text?* Because feedback that feels like a reaction is more fun than feedback that looks like a log entry. Same information, completely different vibe.

## Things to change once it works

- Add the small piezo buzzer (or a tiny servo arm that "slams" a paper door) so the alarm has audio or motion too.
- Swap the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module for the HC-SR04 ultrasonic and compare: ultrasonic gives you a *distance number*, the IR module only gives you a *yes/no*. Same project shape, very different sensor character.
- Add WiFi: have the ESP32 send a "tripped at HH:MM:SS" line to your laptop or to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) over MQTT, so you can see a log of every doorway crossing.
- Mount the module sideways in a doorway with cardboard so it makes a real "laser-style" beam across the threshold.

## Why this is interesting

Almost every "smart" presence sensor in the world - shop door chimes, automatic taps, elevator door re-open - is doing exactly what this circuit does: a beam, a detector, a digital edge, and a reaction. Building the toy version once makes the grown-up versions stop feeling like magic. It's also a near-zero-frustration project: no analog calibration, no flaky timing, no maths - just "something is here / something is not here" with instant visual payoff.
