projects.name: Piggy Bank Coin Counter (TCRT5000 + OLED)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a phone charger or laptop into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the TCRT5000 module, the OLED, and the indicator LED.
projects.description:
A real-world piggy bank that knows how much you've fed it. The TCRT5000 sits in the throat of the slot pointing across the gap; whenever a coin passes between the IR LED and the phototransistor, the module's digital output drops, the ESP32 counts it, the green LED blinks, and the OLED bumps the total along with a cheerful message. The count survives reboots because it is written to the ESP32's flash memory.

## Parts list

- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the screen, stores the count)
- TCRT5000 IR Reflective Tracking Module (the "eye" that catches each coin)
- 0.96" OLED Display, I2C (the running tally and cheer board)
- 5mm green LED + 330R resistor (an instant "I saw that" flash)
- Breadboard + DuPont jumpers (no soldering)

## Wiring notes

- TCRT5000 has four pins: VCC, GND, DO (digital out), AO (analog out). We only use DO.
- Power the TCRT5000 from 3.3V on the ESP32, not 5V. The module's onboard LM393 comparator is happy at 3.3V and that keeps the DO line at 3.3V too - safe for the ESP32 GPIO.
- DO is "active LOW": idle = HIGH, coin overhead = LOW. The onboard pot lets you tune the trigger distance - turn it until the on-board indicator LED just lights when a coin is in position.
- OLED is I2C: SDA = GPIO 21, SCL = GPIO 22 (the ESP32's default I2C pins).
- The green LED's long leg (anode) goes to GPIO 17 through the 330R resistor; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND.
- Common ground everywhere - the sensor module, OLED, and LED all share GND with the ESP32.

## Talking points

- The TCRT5000 is basically an IR flashlight and an IR camera sitting next to each other. The flashlight always shines forward; the camera only "sees" light if something in front bounces some of it back. A coin held a centimetre above the sensor is a great mirror for invisible IR.
- Why "active LOW"? The comparator chip on the module is wired so that "lots of reflected light" pulls the output down to ground. It is the standard convention for these modules and is worth getting used to - it will come back on the IR obstacle modules and the PIR sensors.
- The debounce timer (250 ms) is there because one coin passing through can briefly flicker the sensor twice as it tumbles. We treat anything inside 250 ms as the same coin.
- `Preferences` is the ESP32's tiny built-in key/value store. We save the count every time it changes, so unplugging the bank does not reset the total.

## Things to change once it works

- Build an actual slot: a cardboard tube or a 3D-printed funnel with the TCRT5000 staring across the throat. A short, narrow chute makes the detection rock-solid.
- Add a "session" counter alongside the lifetime total - reset on a button press.
- Switch the cheer text to count up the cash value if you only feed it one coin type ("$0.25", "$0.50"...).
- Pipe the count to MQTT on the (eventually-booted) Orange Pi so the household can race each other to fill their banks.
- Swap DO for AO (analog out) and look at how the reflected-light reading actually changes with coin distance - a great intro to ADCs.

## Why this is interesting

It teaches the difference between a "raw" sensor reading and an "event". The TCRT5000 gives you a continuous on/off signal, but what you really want is one count per coin - which means edge detection, debouncing, and a tiny state machine. Those are the same three ideas that show up in every button, encoder, and motion sensor project, so once they click here they keep paying off.

projects.name: Porch Night-Light (KY-018 dusk-to-dawn fader)
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable; the KY-018 and the LED both run from the Uno's 5V rail.
projects.description:
A pretend porch-light that turns on by itself when the room gets dark. The KY-018 photoresistor watches the ambient light; a yellow LED on the breadboard fades up as the room darkens and fades back down at sunrise - exactly how a real dusk-to-dawn porch bulb behaves, but built on the kitchen table.

## Parts list

- KY-018 Photoresistor Module (the "eye" - an LDR on a little PCB)
- Arduino Uno R3 (5V, 10-bit ADC - perfect for an analog sensor)
- 1x yellow 5mm LED (stands in for a porch bulb; warm yellow looks the part)
- 1x 220R resistor (current limit for the LED)
- Breadboard + a handful of jumpers (3x F-M for the KY-018 module pins, the rest M-M for the LED side)

## Wiring notes

The KY-018 has a 3-pin header that reads, in most clones, `S`, `+`, `-` (signal, power, ground). Use F-M jumpers straight onto those:

- `S` -> Arduino `A0`
- `+` -> Arduino `5V` (the KY-018 wants 5V, not 3.3V - good habit to lock in now, because when you move to the ESP32 you'll need to remember the ESP32's GPIO and Vcc are 3.3V, not 5V)
- `-` -> Arduino `GND`

The LED lives on the breadboard:

- Arduino `D9` (a PWM pin - the `~` symbol is on it) -> 220R resistor -> LED anode (long leg)
- LED cathode (short leg) -> Arduino `GND`

Pin `D9` matters - the sketch fades the LED, and fading needs PWM. If you put it on `D7` instead it can only go full on or full off.

## Talking points

- Why an analog pin (`A0`), not a digital one. The KY-018 doesn't say "dark / not dark"; it says "this much light", as a voltage from 0 to 5V. The Uno's ADC converts that voltage into a number from 0 to 1023, and that's the number we map into "how bright should the LED be".
- Why smoothing. If the porch bulb just looked at the raw reading and turned on whenever it crossed a threshold, every passing shadow would flicker it. The sketch keeps a running average (an exponential moving average, or EMA) so it reacts to "the sun went down" but ignores "a hand briefly waved past". This is the single most advanced trick in the sketch - everything else is map/constrain/analogWrite.
- Why two thresholds (`DARK_START_PERCENT` and `DARK_FULL_PERCENT`) instead of one. Two thresholds give a gentle fade-in region instead of a snap. This is what a real dusk-to-dawn sensor does inside, and it's also what makes the project feel polished instead of toy-like.
- Calibration at startup. KY-018 clones vary - some give a high reading in the dark, some give a low one, and the absolute values depend on the room. Sampling for ~3 seconds at boot while you cover-then-uncover the sensor lets the sketch figure out what "normal" looks like in your room, so you don't have to hardcode magic numbers. If you miss the prompt entirely, the sketch falls back to sensible defaults (200/900) so it still works.
- The polarity knob. Some KY-018 clones read higher as it gets darker; others read lower. The sketch has one constant near the top, `DARK_IS_HIGH`, that picks which. If the porch light is on in daylight and off in the dark, flip it from `true` to `false` and re-upload. One flag, one line - the rest of the code adapts.

## Things to change once it works

- Swap the yellow LED for the blue or green one and watch the same logic work unchanged - the LED colour is "front-end", the logic is "back-end".
- Cover the KY-018 with a cupped hand. The LED should fade up smoothly over half a second or so, not snap. If it snaps, increase `SMOOTHING` toward 0.2 (faster) or decrease it toward 0.01 (slower).
- Add a second LED on `D10` (also PWM) that comes on only when it's *really* dark - call it the "burglar deterrent" porch flood.
- Once Andy has soldered headers on a relay, the LED could be swapped for the 1-channel relay driving a real low-voltage lamp. (Project as written stays solder-free.)
- The KY-018 vs the LM393 photoresistor module: the LM393 board has a comparator on it and gives you a *digital* dark / not-dark output (and a threshold knob). The KY-018 gives you the *analog* reading and lets you decide. That's why this project uses fading - you can't fade off a digital signal.

## Why this is interesting

This is the cleanest possible example of "sensor in, actuator out, brain in the middle". Every home-automation project Andy will ever build is the same shape: read something about the world, decide what to do, change something in the world. Light -> Arduino -> LED is the smallest honest version of that loop, and once it works the same code structure scales straight up to "soil moisture -> ESP32 -> watering pump" or "motion -> ESP32 -> WiFi notification".

projects.name: Laser Tripwire Alarm (LDR + KY-008 pair)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the board's onboard regulator feeds 3.3V to both the laser module and the photoresistor receiver.
projects.description:
## Eye safety - read first

The KY-008 is a real 650nm laser diode module (laser-pointer class, typically rated under 5mW but still hazardous). Even brief direct exposure or a glint off a shiny surface can damage the retina, and the damage is painless and permanent. Before powering the board:

- Never look into the beam or the emitter aperture, not even "just to check it's on". If you need to confirm it works, look at the red dot on a matte surface (a piece of paper, a wall, the white face of the LDR module).
- Never aim the laser at a person, a pet, a window, a mirror, polished metal, or any glossy surface that could bounce a specular reflection back at someone.
- Aim it once with the receiver taped down, then leave it. Treat it like a loaded staple gun: it's pointed somewhere specific, and you don't pick it up to "see where it goes" while live.
- The sketch turns the laser ON as soon as the board boots. Plug power in only after both modules are pointed at each other and taped in place.

## Parts list

- 1x Photoresistor Module (LM393 comparator) - the receiver. It has a built-in pot to set the dark/light threshold and a clean digital DO output.
- 1x KY-008 Red Laser Module (650nm) - the emitter. The narrow beam crosses the doorway and lands on the receiver.
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the receiver, controls the laser, latches the alarm.
- 1x red 5mm LED + 220R resistor - "the wire's been tripped" indicator that stays on.
- 1x tactile push-button - re-arm button to clear the latched alarm.
- Breadboard + DuPont jumpers.

## Wiring notes

Reminder: the laser turns on the moment the ESP32 boots. Finish all wiring, point the laser at the receiver, and tape both modules down BEFORE you plug the USB cable in.

- Both modules run on 3.3V from the ESP32 (the laser module is happy at 3.3V; it's a touch dimmer than at 5V but still very visible at room range).
- The LM393 receiver module has 4 pins: VCC, GND, DO (digital out), AO (analog, ignored here). Only DO is connected to the ESP32.
- The DO pin is **active LOW when bright**. With the laser hitting the LDR, DO reads LOW. When something blocks the beam, DO goes HIGH. The code reflects this exactly.
- The KY-008 has 3 pins in a row. On this clone they are:
  - **S** (signal) -> GPIO 23 on the ESP32. Drive HIGH to turn the beam on.
  - **middle pin** -> **NC, leave disconnected**. Do not feed 3V3 here; it is not a power input on this module.
  - **-** (GND) -> GND rail.
- The LED goes from GPIO 22 through a 220R resistor to GND. Standard ESP32 LED hookup.
- The re-arm button connects GPIO 4 to GND. The internal pull-up does the rest.

**Aiming and calibration**

1. With the USB cable still unplugged, lay out the laser and the receiver across the doorway and tape them down so they can't drift. Point the emitter at the white LDR window on the receiver.
2. Plug in USB. The laser turns on automatically. Do not look at the emitter; look at the receiver to confirm the red dot landed on the white window.
3. Turn the blue trim-pot on the receiver module slowly. Its onboard signal LED will flip ON when dark, OFF when bright. Find the spot where the laser-on state is **just barely** counted as "bright" (LED just off). That's your most sensitive setting.
4. Wave a finger through the beam (not your eye). The red alarm LED should latch on, and serial should print `>>> TRIPWIRE BROKEN <<<`.
5. Press the button to re-arm.

## Talking points

- **A tripwire is just a "before vs after" test.** The laser doesn't measure anything fancy. It just gives the receiver one easy thing to see. When that one thing disappears, we know something passed through.
- **Why latch the alarm?** A real intruder is only in the beam for a few milliseconds. If the LED only lit while the beam was broken, you'd never see it. Latching means: once tripped, stay tripped until a human acknowledges it.
- **Two modules talking through air.** There are no wires between the laser and the receiver - the beam itself is the signal. That's the same idea as a TV remote, a barcode scanner, or fibre-optic internet, just slower.
- **The LM393 comparator on the receiver.** The little chip on the module compares the LDR's voltage to whatever the pot is set to and gives a clean HIGH/LOW. Without it, you'd be reading a noisy analog value and writing your own threshold code.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a piezo buzzer in parallel with the alarm LED for an audible siren.
- Drive the laser through a transistor and **pulse** it at 1 kHz, then have the receiver only count the alarm if the pulse goes missing. That defeats someone shining a flashlight at the receiver to fool it.
- Bounce the beam off a small mirror so the laser and receiver sit on the same side of the doorway. Easier to install, looks more like a spy movie. (Mirror placement still needs the eye-safety rules: don't aim it where a reflection could find a face.)
- Have the ESP32 publish the trip event over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once the Pi is booted).
- Add a 5-second arming countdown so you can leave the room before the tripwire goes hot.

## Why this is interesting

It's the first project in the kit where two separate active components have to physically agree on something across empty space. The wiring on the breadboard is short and friendly, but the real "circuit" is invisible. That makes the debugging satisfying: nudge the laser, watch the latch hold, press re-arm, and you've built a tiny security system out of a 50-cent LDR module and a laser pointer.

projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Optical Slot / Speed Sensor (the protagonist - an IR LED facing a phototransistor across a small gap)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C, SSD1306)
- 1x Breadboard
- A handful of male-male and female-male jumpers
- Coins, popsicle-stick wedges, or strips of paper to drop through the slot

No resistors needed - the slot sensor module already has its own pull-up and current-limit resistors on board, and the OLED is I2C with internal pull-ups on the breakout. No LEDs in this build, so no current-limiting resistor either.

## Wiring notes

The slot sensor has 4 pins: `VCC`, `GND`, `D0` (digital out), and sometimes `A0` (analog). We only care about `D0`. When nothing is in the slot, the beam reaches the phototransistor and `D0` sits HIGH. The instant something blocks the beam, `D0` snaps LOW. That falling edge is what we count.

- Sensor `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`
- Sensor `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`
- Sensor `D0` -> ESP32 `GPIO 4`
- OLED `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`
- OLED `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`
- OLED `SDA` -> ESP32 `GPIO 21`
- OLED `SCL` -> ESP32 `GPIO 22`

Orient the slot **vertically** so coins fall down through the gap under gravity - tape the sensor module to the edge of a book or shoebox with the U-shape opening pointing up. A horizontal slot won't work; coins need somewhere to fall.

If drops sometimes don't register even though they clearly passed through the slot, try moving the sensor `VCC` wire from `3V3` to `VIN` (the 5V USB rail on the NodeMCU). The LM393 comparator on these slot modules is spec'd 3.3-5V, but some clones produce a cleaner, sharper falling edge with a full 5V supply. The `D0` output is still safe to feed into a 3.3V ESP32 GPIO - it's just a slow logic-level signal pulled to whatever rail the module runs on, and ESP32 inputs tolerate that fine in practice for this use.

## Talking points

- "What is an interrupt?" Most code in a loop is busy checking things. An interrupt is the chip dropping everything the moment a pin changes, running a tiny piece of code, then jumping back. For something as fast as a coin falling through a 5 mm gap, polling in `loop()` could miss it. An interrupt cannot.
- "Why a `volatile` keyword?" The compiler usually assumes nothing else changes a variable behind its back. `volatile` tells it "no, this can change at any moment because an interrupt might touch it" so it always re-reads from memory.
- "What's debounce?" A coin doesn't break the beam cleanly - it can flicker the signal a few times in a few milliseconds. We ignore any second trigger that comes within 40 ms of the previous one.
- "What does `readSnapshot()` do?" An interrupt can fire halfway through `loop()` reading the shared variables, which would give us a torn, half-updated value. `readSnapshot()` briefly turns interrupts off, copies everything in one go, then turns interrupts back on. That's a "critical section".

## Things to change once it works

- Tape a piece of card with evenly-spaced slits to the side of a spinning fan and you've turned the same sensor into a tachometer (RPM meter). Count slits per second, divide by slit count, multiply by 60.
- Add the buzzer from the kit (or a piezo if you grab one) so each coin makes a beep.
- Make a 10-second window: how many coins can you drop in 10 seconds? Reset on button press.
- Log each drop's timestamp to the Serial Monitor and paste into a spreadsheet to graph drop intervals.

## Why this is interesting

This is the first build in the kit where timing accuracy matters. Polling in `loop()` works fine for buttons and slow sensors, but the moment you start measuring fast physical events - a coin drop, a fan blade, a moving belt - you need interrupts. Once Andy sees the count tick up reliably even when he drops three coins in quick succession, the "why use an interrupt" lesson sticks. Same hardware later becomes the speedometer for a Lego car, the slot encoder on a robot wheel, or a beam-break alarm across a doorway.

projects.name: Stealth Timer - hold still or the LED dies
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered over its USB-C cable from a laptop or a 5 V USB phone charger; the PIR sensor, OLED and LEDs all run from the ESP32's onboard 5 V and 3.3 V rails.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x HC-SR505 Mini PIR Motion Sensor (the star: a tiny PIR with a clear plastic dome that fires HIGH when it sees a warm body move)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C)
- 1x 5mm green LED (glows while you are holding still)
- 1x 5mm red LED (flashes when you twitch)
- 2x 330R resistors (one in series with each LED)
- 1x breadboard, plus a handful of M-M and F-M jumpers

## Wiring notes

The HC-SR505 has only three pins: `VCC`, `OUT`, `GND`. It accepts 5 V on VCC and its OUT line idles at 0 V and pulses HIGH (about 3.0 V on this module) when triggered, which the ESP32's 3.3 V GPIO can read safely without a level shifter.

Power the PIR and the OLED from the ESP32's `5V` pin (which is the USB rail when you have the board plugged into your laptop). Tie every ground - PIR, OLED, both LEDs - back to the ESP32's `GND`.

The OLED is I2C and goes on the ESP32's default I2C pins: `SDA = GPIO 21`, `SCL = GPIO 22`. The PIR's OUT goes to `GPIO 13`. The green LED's anode goes through a 330R resistor to `GPIO 18`, the red LED's anode goes through its own 330R resistor to `GPIO 19`, and both cathodes go to ground.

Important first-time gotcha: the HC-SR505 needs about 30 seconds after power-up to settle - it will output garbage during that window. The sketch handles this for you by showing a "Warming up PIR" screen and slow-pulsing the red LED. Stay out of view while that's running.

## Talking points

- The HC-SR505 doesn't see *light*. It sees *infrared heat moving across its field of view*. That's why holding still in front of it - even with your eyes open - makes it go quiet.
- Inside that little plastic dome is a Fresnel lens. It splits the view into zones; the sensor only triggers when warmth crosses from one zone into another.
- The OUT pin is digital, not analog. There's no "how much motion" reading - just yes or no.
- The ESP32 is reading the pin millions of times per second, but we only act once per loop with a tiny delay - that's enough.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer that beeps softly the longer your streak gets, so you have to hold still through rising tension.
- Show a tiny "high score" bar graph on the OLED that grows with your best time.
- Save the best streak to ESP32 flash (Preferences library) so it survives a reboot.
- Add a second HC-SR505 aimed sideways and only count "frontal" motion - turns the game into a stealth competition for two people.

## Why this is interesting

PIR sensors are the everyday motion detector you've seen a thousand times - in burglar alarms, in motion-activated lights at the supermarket, in automatic taps. The HC-SR505 is the tiniest, cheapest version of that hardware, and it has exactly one job: tell you whether a warm thing just moved. Turning that single bit of information into a little game is a satisfying way to feel how a real sensor behaves: the warm-up window, the lens zones, the way it doesn't care about a glass of hot water but cares a lot about your hand.

projects.name: Storm Glass - 3-hour pressure trend forecaster
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered from a laptop / phone-charger USB cable; the ESP32's 3.3 V pin supplies both the BMP280 and the OLED through the breadboard rails.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- **GY-BMP280 Barometric Pressure Sensor** - the protagonist. A tiny Bosch chip that measures absolute air pressure to about +-1 Pa. Pressure is what weather forecasters actually watch: rising pressure usually means fair weather coming, falling pressure means a storm coming.
- **ESP32 NodeMCU-32S** - reads the sensor and drives the screen.
- **0.96" OLED Display (I2C)** - shows the current pressure, a big up/down arrow, and a one-word forecast.
- **Breadboard** plus **M-M** and **F-M jumper wires** - both modules share the same two I2C wires (SDA + SCL) plus 3.3 V and GND, so the breadboard just acts as a 4-rail splitter.

## Wiring notes

Both modules are I2C. That means four wires total from the ESP32, no matter how many I2C devices you add:

- ESP32 `3V3` -> breadboard `+` rail -> BMP280 `VCC` and OLED `VCC`
- ESP32 `GND` -> breadboard `-` rail -> BMP280 `GND` and OLED `GND`
- ESP32 `GPIO21` (SDA) -> BMP280 `SDA` and OLED `SDA`
- ESP32 `GPIO22` (SCL) -> BMP280 `SCL` and OLED `SCL`

Both boards already have I2C pull-up resistors on them, so no extra resistors are needed.

The BMP280 sits at I2C address `0x76` on most GY-BMP280 clones. A few clones are at `0x77`. The code tries both so you do not have to care.

## Talking points

- **What is air pressure?** The weight of all the air above you, pressing down. At sea level on an average day it is about 1013 hPa. When a storm front moves in, that number drops; when it leaves, it rises.
- **Why a 3-hour delta?** Weather services use the 3-hour pressure tendency as the basic forecast signal. One single reading tells you nothing - it is the *change over time* that predicts the weather.
- **Why a ring buffer?** We keep 180 readings (one per minute for 3 hours). Instead of growing a list forever, we overwrite the oldest slot every minute. This is the same trick used in audio buffers and game replay systems.
- **I2C is a shared bus.** The OLED and the BMP280 use the *same* two wires. They get along because they have different addresses (`0x3C` vs `0x76`).

## Things to change once it works

- Add a 24-hour delta too (just bump `HISTORY_MINUTES` to 1440 and add a second arrow).
- Plot the history as a tiny line graph across the bottom of the OLED.
- Publish the pressure to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is online, so the Hallway Weather Window project can show it alongside temperature.
- Calibrate to altitude: feed in the local altitude and the sketch can spit out sea-level-equivalent pressure that matches what weather.gov reports.
- Add a piezo buzzer that beeps when the forecast crosses into "Storm!" so you get a warning even when you are not looking at the screen.

## Why this is interesting

This is a real instrument, not a toy. The BMP280 is sensitive enough that you can *see* the pressure change when you walk up a flight of stairs (about -0.4 hPa per 4 metres). And the 3-hour delta really does predict weather - leave it on the kitchen counter for a week and you will start trusting the arrow more than the phone app.

It is also the cleanest example in the kit of the I2C-bus idea: two completely different chips, from two different vendors, sharing two wires. Once Andy is comfortable with this, adding a third or fourth I2C sensor is just plugging it into the same rails.

projects.name: Pocket Battery Health Monitor (OLED + LEDs)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 powered by laptop USB. OLED runs from the ESP32's 3.3V rail; LEDs are driven by GPIO. The voltage module is passive (just resistors) and draws no power. The battery under test connects only to the module's input screws.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- Voltage Sensor Module (0-25V divider) - the star: a tiny board with two resistors (30k + 7.5k) that shrinks a DC voltage down to something the ESP32's 3.3V ADC can survive. The module is rated up to 25V at the input, but as you'll see in Talking points, the ESP32's ADC only stays linear up to about 12V of input. Above that the screen number goes wonky.
- ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the divider's output on GPIO 34 and drives the screen
- 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - shows the live number, a bar graph, and the word HEALTHY / LOW / DEAD
- 1x green LED with a 220R limiter and 1x red LED with a 330R limiter - instant "go / no-go" feedback even before you look at the screen. Green gets the smaller resistor on purpose - green LEDs need a higher forward voltage than red, so at 3.3V drive a 330R would leave it visibly dim.
- Breadboard + jumpers - no soldering

A 9V battery (or any low-voltage DC source up to ~12V you want to measure) is the **device under test**. You touch its terminals to the voltage module's input. The whole project itself is powered through the ESP32's USB cable. The voltage module is a passive resistor pair, so it draws no power of its own and does not need a VCC connection.

## Wiring notes

The voltage module has two sides:

- **Screw-terminal side (input):** the thing you measure. The screws are labelled `VCC` (positive) and `GND` (negative). Andy connects the battery being tested here.
- **Pin-header side (output):** three pins labelled `S` (signal, the divided-down voltage), `+` (unused, leave alone), and `-` (ground). The `-` pin **must share ground with the ESP32** or the reading is meaningless.

So the wiring story is: battery `+` and `-` go into the screw terminals. `S` goes to ESP32 GPIO 34. The module's `-` pin goes to ESP32 GND. Same-ground is the rule that makes the whole thing work.

OLED is normal I2C: VCC to 3.3V (most 0.96" I2C OLEDs have an onboard regulator and accept 3.3-5V; the ESP32's 3.3V rail is fine), GND to GND, SDA to GPIO 21, SCL to GPIO 22.

The green LED gets a 220R resistor in series with its anode (long leg). The red LED gets a 330R. Cathodes both to GND.

**Do not** feed more than 25V into the module, and **do not** ever connect AC, mains, or the wall. This project is for batteries and bench DC supplies only.

## Talking points

- The voltage module is just a **voltage divider**: two resistors in series. The "S" pin sits at the junction and carries a fraction of the input voltage. With 30k on top and 7.5k on the bottom, the ratio is 5:1 - feed 25V in, get 5V at S. Feed 9V in, get 1.8V at S. The ESP32 then multiplies by 5 in software to recover the original number.
- **Why the real measurement ceiling is ~12V, not 25V.** With the attenuation setting we use (`ADC_11db`), the ESP32 ADC is only linear from about 0.15V up to about 2.45V at the pin. Multiply 2.45V by the divider's 5:1 ratio and you get ~12V at the input. Above that, the ADC saturates and the displayed number flattens out - the module isn't damaged, but the reading is no longer trustworthy. The code shows a `>12V (clip)` warning when that happens. For 9V alkalines, 12V SLA at rest, and 18650 cells, you're comfortably inside the linear band.
- Why GPIO 34? It's an **input-only ADC pin** on ESP32 and it's also on ADC1, which (unlike ADC2) keeps working while WiFi is on. Good habit for future projects.
- The ESP32 ADC is famously a little non-linear, so the code includes a `CAL` fudge factor (default 1.00). Once everything works, Andy can compare the OLED reading to a real multimeter on the same battery, and nudge `CAL` until they agree **inside the band he actually cares about** (e.g. 6V-10V for testing 9V alkalines).

## Things to change once it works

- Change `HEALTHY_VOLTS` to suit a different battery. For a 12V lead-acid you'd use ~12.2V (right at the edge of the linear range, so multimeter-calibrate carefully). For a single Li-ion 18650 cell you'd use ~3.5V (well inside the safe range).
- Add a third "warning" yellow LED for the in-between band.
- Add WiFi and post the voltage to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is booted, turning this into a real battery-monitoring node.
- Plot voltage over time on the OLED instead of just a level bar - sample once a second into a 128-wide ring buffer and you get a free oscilloscope.
- To extend the measurement range past ~12V on this exact module, you'd need to either add another resistor in series upstream (extending the divider) or switch the attenuation setting on a different pin - both are good follow-up experiments.

## Why this is interesting

Voltage measurement is the most fundamental thing a sensor can do, and yet it's hidden inside almost every other module - the joystick, the photoresistor, the soil sensor, all secretly produce a voltage and let the microcontroller's ADC read it. Building this project makes that hidden machinery visible. After this, Andy will look at every analog sensor in the kit and recognise the same trick: "it's just a voltage I'm reading and converting to a number."

It's also genuinely useful. Every project from here on uses batteries or DC supplies, and now Andy has a meter he built himself that tells him whether the battery in his hand still has juice. And the "ADC only goes linear to ~2.45V at the pin" lesson is one of those gotchas every ESP32 project eventually trips over - better to meet it here with a clear printout than to chase a phantom bug later.

projects.name: Raindrop Reporter - live wetness on OLED
projects.power_supply: Powered from a USB-C cable plugged into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S. The board's 3V3 pin supplies the raindrop sensor module, the OLED, and the LED.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- 1x Raindrop Sensor (the comb board + its little LM393 amplifier board)
- 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
- 1x 0.96" OLED display (I2C, address 0x3C)
- 1x Blue 5mm LED
- 1x 330R resistor (current limit for the LED)
- 1x Breadboard
- Jumper wires (a mix of M-M and F-M)

## Wiring notes

The raindrop sensor comes in two pieces joined by a 2-wire lead: a flat comb-trace board (the bit that gets wet) and a small amplifier board with the 4-pin header. The amplifier board is where everything plugs in.

- Sensor `VCC` -> ESP32 `3V3`. The module is happy at 3.3V; do NOT use 5V here even though the silkscreen allows it - the analog output would swing past what the ESP32 ADC tolerates.
- Sensor `GND` -> ESP32 `GND`.
- Sensor `AO` (analog out) -> ESP32 `GPIO34`. GPIO34 is input-only and lives on ADC1, which keeps working while WiFi is on - a small but important detail on the ESP32.
- Ignore the `DO` (digital out) pin. The on-board pot only sets the threshold for `DO`; we read the analog signal directly so we don't have to twist the trimmer.
- OLED: `VCC -> 3V3`, `GND -> GND`, `SDA -> GPIO21`, `SCL -> GPIO22`. These are the ESP32's default I2C pins.
- Blue LED: long leg (anode) goes through the 330R resistor to `GPIO5`, short leg (cathode) to `GND`.

The raindrop sensor is "wet = low value, dry = high value". That's because the comb traces work as a variable resistor: water bridges them, the resistance drops, and the on-board divider pulls AO toward ground.

## Talking points

- Why GPIO34? Show Sandy the ESP32 pinout. ADC2 pins go quiet whenever WiFi turns on - we picked an ADC1 pin so we don't get bitten by that later.
- The `classify()` thresholds were guessed. The real ones come from watching the Serial Monitor while flicking water on the board: write down the value when dry, when finger-damp, when a drop is sitting on it, and when it's fully submerged. Edit the four constants at the top to match.
- Averaging 8 samples is a tiny but useful trick - one stray reading would make the display jitter between MISTY and WET every quarter second otherwise.

## Things to change once it works

- Add a buzzer that beeps when state crosses into SOAKED - then it's a basement-flood alarm.
- Log the state changes with `millis()` over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi MQTT broker, so you've got a record of when it rained.
- Use the `DO` pin instead of `AO` and skip the OLED - simpler "rain or no rain" version for the XIAO ESP32-C3.
- Make the wetness bar pulse faster the wetter it gets - visible feedback without needing to read numbers.

## Why this is interesting

The raindrop sensor is the cheapest physical-world-touching sensor you have - it's literally two interleaved copper combs and a comparator. This project shows the full beginner-friendly chain: a noisy real-world analog signal, smoothed by averaging, classified into human-readable buckets, then displayed two different ways (text + bar graph + LED). It's also the simplest hook into "act on the world": once you can confidently detect rain, the same code pattern works for soil moisture, water level, and any other resistive/analog sensor in the kit.

projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable. The Uno's onboard 5V rail then feeds the water sensor, the LCD, and the LED resistors.
projects.description:
## Parts list

- Arduino Uno R3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the LCD and LEDs)
- Water Level Sensor (resistive comb - the protagonist; more water touching the combs = lower resistance = higher analog reading)
- LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (shows a live bar graph and a percent number)
- 3 LEDs (red, yellow, green) - "stoplight" progress indicator
- 3x 330R resistors (current-limiters, one per LED)
- 1x 1M resistor (pull-down on the sensor's signal pin so the reading falls cleanly to 0 when dry)
- Breadboard + a small handful of M-M and F-M jumper wires (one pack of each is plenty)
- A glass of water (the "tub") to dip the sensor into

## Wiring notes

- The water sensor has three pins labelled `+`, `-`, `S`. `+` goes to Arduino 5V, `-` goes to Arduino GND, and `S` is the analog output that goes to Arduino A0.
- The 1M pull-down resistor goes from A0 to GND. This is the "why doesn't it read zero when dry?" fix - without it, the floating input drifts and shows random numbers when there's no water.
- LCD I2C backpack: only 4 wires. VCC -> 5V, GND -> GND, SDA -> A4, SCL -> A5. (On the Uno, A4 and A5 double as the I2C bus.)
- LEDs: each LED's long leg (anode) goes through a 330R resistor to its Arduino pin. Short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Red on D5, Yellow on D6, Green on D7.
- IMPORTANT - do not submerge the top half of the water sensor board. Only the gold combs should ever touch water. The exposed components above will corrode in days if they get wet.

## Talking points

- Why a "resistive comb" sensor? It's just two interleaved bare-copper tracks. Water between them conducts a tiny bit of current. More water covering the combs = more conductive paths in parallel = more current = bigger number from `analogRead`. It's the same trick the Soil Moisture Sensor uses, just shaped to read a vertical column instead of a flat patch.
- Why the 1M pull-down? An Arduino analog input that isn't connected to anything acts like a tiny antenna - it picks up mains hum and reads random numbers. Tying it weakly to ground through 1M forces it to read 0 when the sensor is dry, but lets the sensor easily overpower it when water is present.
- The LCD updates fast on purpose - you can dip the sensor in and out and watch the bar graph respond immediately. That tight feedback loop is what makes it fun.

## Things to change once it works

- Calibrate `WET_MAX` to your actual glass of water. Dip the sensor all the way and read the value over Serial - that's your real max. Beginner-typical values land between 500 and 700.
- Add a buzzer that beeps once when the green "FULL" zone is reached - that turns it from a visual toy into an actual "tub is full, come turn the tap off" alarm.
- Swap to the ESP32 and publish the level over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi hub. Same sensor wiring, different brain.
- Try the Raindrop Sensor on the same code with no changes - it's electrically identical, just a flatter comb shape.

## Why this is interesting

This is the cheapest, simplest possible "is there water there?" sensor, and it teaches a real-world lesson the first time you use it: analog inputs don't read clean zero when nothing's connected. Fixing that with a pull-down resistor is a habit that carries over to almost every analog sensor you'll ever use. And visually, dipping a probe into a glass and watching a bar graph fill up is hugely satisfying - especially for a 10-year-old.
